WorldViewer.installWater starts a javax.swing.Timer at 120 ms that calls scene.scrollWater(elapsedSeconds) every tick; the clock is stopped in close() alongside the glide timer, and is never installed when the world has no pond (scene.pondCount() == 0) or the feature is off — so a world without water costs zero timers and zero graph writes. scrollWater catches every RuntimeException | Error from the generator write and returns, making a torn-down universe silence the animation rather than drop the EDT. 10 new headless cases (WorldSceneTest 7: the shipped pond collects, the feature switch gates collection to zero, a zero/negative extent costs a pond not the frame, pondSeat composes cell-then- record, a zero-length axis leaves the plane flat, a real axis reaches the matrix; WaterArtTest 3: planeS/planeT tile the plane not the world, the scroll is the planes' constant term alone, a whole tile later the offset has wrapped to zero, and a NaN clock still hands a usable plane). What remains probe-side is whether the fixed pipeline honours an object-linear generation past one tile repeat and whether the ripple is visible at a real pond's depth.
  • Walking through a room now says something — roadmap P1.2, triggers wired (wonderland-common, wonderland-renderer, lg3d-apps) — TriggerZone and TriggerField had shipped as a tested enter/exit edge detector that nothing drove: a walker could cross every doorway in a world and the world never learned it. WorldScene.triggerZones() now derives one zone per placed cell straight from the inventory the walk already builds — footprint as the horizontal half-extents, blocking height as the vertical band — deliberately *derived* rather than authored, because the 2006 .mtg format carries no trigger record and inventing a schema nothing produces repeats the CellSnapshot mistake. TriggerWatcher is the small stateful layer the renderer holds between frames: it primes the room the walker starts in (so entry is not a spurious "enter" on the first frame), forwards each crossed edge with the walker's real pose, and swallows a listener that throws so a behaviour bug is silence, never a dropped frame. WorldViewer installs it once the walk's first pose is chosen and drives it at the single place the eye is ever written, behind the new lg.wonderland.trigger switch (WorldFeatures), walk-only, and inert for a world with no volumes or no listener — so the pre-P1.2 walk is byte-identical. The edge reaches P5 through the seam the dependency rule forces: the renderer cannot import Mandela, so WorldRender — the walk-in host already running the world's behaviour.mnd for cell labels — attaches a listener and WorldBehavior.triggerNote binds trigger/action/x/y/z for one crossing, its answer shown in the window title through a new WorldViewer.setStatus; a world whose behaviour was written only for cells reads nothing here and stays silent. 13 new headless cases (TriggerWatcherTest 5, WorldSceneTest zonesOf 2, WorldBehaviorTest trigger crossings 6): crossing a zone fires exactly one enter then one exit and never a per-frame echo, the start room is primed not fired, a listener that throws cannot stop the edges after it, an empty world primes no zones, every placed cell becomes one zone with its own footprint and band, and an enter/exit crossing reaches a real Mandela.eval with its pose bound while a null, blank, throwing or empty-valued script all collapse to no note. The crossing decision, the priming and the behaviour note are headless-proven; the title changing while a person walks is the probe-side half, exactly as P4.1 left its on-screen ear.
  • The world writes itself down — roadmap P5.4, autosave wired (wonderland-server) — CellSnapshot shipped as save/restore that nothing called: a memory of where a chair was slid that only a hand could invoke, because the WorldModel re-seeds from its module art every boot and every applyMove since then lived only in RAM. WorldAutosaver is the policy that runs it without one — it polls a new WorldModel.revision() counter (a monotonic AtomicLong bumped by every add/graft/move/remove and never by a read, so a busy-but-unchanged world costs no disk traffic and an untouched world writes no file at all) and, once the world has settled for one quiet interval, writes the snapshot; a failed write (disk full, read-only mount) is logged and leaves the world dirty so the next tick retries rather than silently forgetting where anything is, because an autosave that takes the running server down over its own bookkeeping is worse than a noisy retry. The whole judgement — dirty?, settled?, did it land? — is decided against an injected instant, so it is unit-tested headlessly; the thin WorldSnapshotService bean is the only half that reads a real clock, giving the saver a @Scheduled beat (@EnableScheduling) plus a restore-on-boot, and it stays inert until an operator names wonderland.server.snapshot.path — the blank default means no restore, no beat, no file, exactly the pre-P5.4 server, so the empty-world socket test and every existing boot stand untouched. A torn snapshot on boot is logged and skipped, not fatal. 9 new headless cases (WorldAutosaverTest 6, WorldSnapshotServiceTest 3): an untouched world writes nothing, a change waits for the quiet interval, a 0.1f move round-trips bit-identical through the snapshot, a failed write leaves the world dirty for retry, a shutdown flush ignores the throttle, the revision counts only mutations never reads, and the bean itself is inert on a blank path, restores and rewrites on a named one, and forgives a torn snapshot on boot.
  • The server fans a move to its audience, not the whole world — roadmap P5.4, wired (wonderland-server) — InterestManager had shipped as a tested kernel that nothing consulted: ProtocolRouter.broadcastMove fanned to registry.all(), so every connected session learned every event. A MovableMessage on a session's OWN view cell now re-homes that session's watch (interest.watch(id, x, y, z, WATCH_RADIUS)), and broadcastMove fans to audienceFor(eventPlace, cellReach) instead — the moved cell's event radius comes from its authored spherical bounds when it has them, else a documented default. The gate is deliberately conservative: the mover always receives its own echo (client-side suppression depends on it), and a session with no registered watch still receives everything, so before any avatar has walked the fan-out is byte-identical to the pre-P5.4 broadcast and every existing multiplayer, loopback and socket-integration test stands untouched; spatial filtering engages only once avatars move. A cache detach forgets the departed watch, so a ghost is never a recipient. World chat is deliberately not filtered — it is addressed to the environment cell every session listens on, so it is a global relay by design, not an interest event. 5 new headless cases (ProtocolRouterInterestTest): the default-open rule, an avatar walk tracking its watch while an unrelated furniture move does not, a move near one avatar reaching it but not a tracked one a kilometre away, a tracked avatar walking into range and starting to hear, and a departure stopping the tracking.
  • Per-pixel GPU lighting reaches the screen — roadmap P2.2 / P0.1, connected and measured (wonderland-renderer) — an earlier pass filed GLSL lighting as a platform impossibility and left J3dMeshFactory's shader wiring "deliberately unapplied." Four probes on the repo's live X:0 / GL 4.6 radeonsi context proved otherwise and settled exactly what this Jogamp 1.7.2 fork can and cannot do: a scene Light never reaches a custom program (gl_LightSource[0] reads GL's default even with a correctly bounded DirectionalLight — WlProbe39), so the key is handed to the program as its OWN lightDirection/lightColor/ambientColor uniforms, which ShaderAttributeSet + program.setShaderAttrNames(...) deliver alongside one TextureUnitState-bound sampler2D (WlProbe40); the corrected production Blinn-Phong GLSL then shades per fragment — a lit quad facing the key reads (255,255,255), a grazing one the (31,31,31) ambient floor (WlProbe41) — but the fork binds exactly ONE texture per program (a second sampler2D re-reads unit 0 — WlProbe42), so a material lights from its diffuse and the normal/spec stages stay compiled and unapplied until a direct-JOGL pass binds its own samplers. buildShaderAppearance is now live behind a triply-conservative gate — the lg.wonderland.shader switch (OFF by default), MaterialAppearance.lit(), and a resolved diffuse texture — so a pre-lit world stays byte-identical to every prior run; WlProbe43 drove the shipping createShape and measured the grading through the production path, not a hand-rolled program. J3dMeshFactory.setLightRig lets WorldScene push its key so the CPU bake and the GPU route answer to one light, and refuses a degenerate (zero/NaN) direction rather than blacking out every lit surface. 3 new headless cases (J3dMeshFactoryShaderGateTest) pin the safety of the gate — the route off-by-default and the rig refusal — the pixels themselves being the probe's claim.
  • The remaining roadmap kernels walk into the live desktop — wiring pass, P0.2 / P1.1 / P3.1 / P4.1 / P5.1, connected (wonderland-renderer, lg3d-apps) — the P0.1 pass named five features still unreachable from a running world because the frame path produced no eye or bounds to feed them; this pass produces them. WorldScene builds a WorldInventory of every mounted cell (id, centre, footprint, blocking height) and wraps each cell's Link in a Switch gate, so cullTo(eye) (P0.2) opens what the world's own WorldPVS says is visible and shuts the rest each time the eye moves, and blockStep(...) (P1.1) seeds an AvatarCollider over the inventory's obstacles so a wall stops a step and slides the walker along its face instead of passing through it. WorldViewer is where the frame meets them: every eye write culls and re-points the audio listener, the arrow keys and WASD resolve through blockStep, FollowRig (P3.1) glides the eye toward its target with the rig's frame-rate-independent smoothing rather than teleporting, and AudioManager/JavaSoundBackend (P4.1) put the ear at that same pose — silent where a machine has no device. P5.1 was already live: WorldRender reads one behaviour script per world through the cached store and lets it re-word each cell's name over the real Mandela.eval, falling back to the authored label on any failure. All four consult WorldFeatures once per use, so -Dlg.wonderland.features=off returns the window to exactly the pre-wiring keyboard-and-void walk, byte for byte. 8 new headless cases (WorldInventoryTest) prove the arithmetic the live path runs on — the PVS keeps a near cell and drops one on the far side of the world, a wall stops a walker and names itself, an unauthored cell is a room not a degenerate zero, and an empty world is the identity for every question. The cull/light pixel delta on a real card stays a WlProbe sentence — the scene-graph Switch and baked colour need a live GL context no headless CI has — and this pass claims no pixel it cannot prove; what it proves is that the kernels now stand on the path a person walks.
  • The lighting rig is wired into the live desktop, and the world is no longer one flat colour — roadmap P0.1, connected (wonderland-common, wonderland-renderer, wonderland-desktop) — the kernels this roadmap shipped over the past weeks were real, tested and reachable only from a probe, so a person launching Wonderland saw exactly what they always saw. This is the first of the wiring passes that puts them in the running path, starting with the one whose pixels can be argued about. J3dMeshFactory now writes a light factor into GeometryArray.COLOR_3 for every shape it builds and puts a textured surface under MODULATE instead of DECAL, because the two measurements in build-gradle/scratch/WlProbe32/33 proved the alternative is not a preference: on this fork a scene-graph Light changes no pixel at all (a red Material answered (46,5,5) with a full-white AmbientLight and the same (46,5,5) with no light in the universe — that is GL's own 0.2 global ambient, and the diffuse term contributes nothing), while a vertex colour *is* honoured and DECAL throws it away. BakedRig holds that arithmetic as a pure class with the calibration recorded in it, defaulting to a gentle 0.72 ambient + 0.28 key rather than an offline renderer's deeper rig, because the shipped textures already carry the server's own bake and a deeper rig would darken the whole world by half; the brightest face is authored-exact by construction. Proven with pixels, not a test count (WlProbe34, one textured quad built through the production createShape with a real image served through TextureSource): with the feature off the surface reads back as 2 colours — flat, the complaint itself — and with it on, 39 distinct colours grading 229 → 199 across the same face, nothing brighter than authored and nothing blackened. WorldFeatures (lg.wonderland.lighting|culling|collision|audio|camera|behaviour|water, master lg.wonderland.features) is the single vocabulary every wiring pass consults, defaulting to ON so a wired feature is actually reachable, and WonderlandDesktop.installRenderer() logs what it read, so the console is evidence rather than a guess. 19 new headless cases (BakedRigTest 13, WorldFeaturesTest 6). Still not wired, and now stated as such rather than implied: culling, collision, audio, camera and behaviour each need an eye or a bounds source the live path does not yet produce.
  • Environment reflection and refraction, as arithmetic and a probe-gated plan — roadmap P2.5 (added scope) (wonderland-renderer) — reflection and refraction were never in the original roadmap; they name beside the water (P2.3) and every glossy surface as the missing "modern 3D" beat. EnvMapKernel is that beat as arithmetic on float[] vectors and packed ARGB pixels with nothing but java.base: the reflect vector, Snell's refraction whose total-internal- reflection past the critical angle answers null (no transmitted ray exists — the same fact the fragment program reads as a zero-length refract() and resolves by falling back to reflection), the Schlick fresnel that walks from F0 head-on to a full mirror at the horizon (why water is a mirror in the distance), the canonical cube-map face-and-uv a direction samples, and two blends whose coverage == 0 is the exact base pixel — the mirror of BloomKernel's strength-zero identity every "glossy toggle" will one day lean on. EnvironmentPlan repeats P2.2's ceiling in a second feature's voice: Java 3D 1.7.2's fixed pipeline can bind a cube texture but cannot compute a per-fragment fresnel blend or a bent lookup, so an environment material takes SHADER *only* when a probe validated the fork's shader API, else FIXED with the lost effects named — and it reuses ShaderAppearancePlan.Capability, so one host answers "is the shader path live" for both. MaterialAppearance now carries a cube-map path, a reflectivity and an index of refraction through a full 15-argument constructor (the 5-, 10- and 12-arg forms delegate unchanged, reflectivity clamps to [0,1], a non-positive ior reads as no bend and blank paths store null), so a material with no cube map and ior == 1 asks for nothing and no pre-P2.5 world loses a pixel. The GLSL 1.20 environment fragment ships with the decision and asserts it names the same reflect/refract/ Schlick operators the kernel computes. 21 new headless cases (EnvMapKernelTest 10, EnvironmentPlanTest 7, MaterialAppearanceTest +4); binding a live cube map and running the program on WorldScene's glossy cells stays a WlProbe sentence on a real card, and this commit claims no pixel it cannot prove.
  • The server session layer gains its three missing judgements — roadmap P5.4 (wonderland-server) — the wire is real and the session table is real, but a transport cannot answer three questions for itself: who should hear this event, where things were before the reboot, and may this caller be that person at all. InterestManager keeps one watch per session — place plus a radius of ear — and answers audienceFor(place, eventRadius) with the union rule: an event's own footprint widens a listener's reach, never narrows it; squared-distance compares, a moved session *replaces* its watch (an avatar that walked away stops hearing the room it left), a departed one is gone from the next audience, and NaN places are refused loudly because a NaN comparison silently excludes everyone. Deliberately an O(n) scan over sessions, not a WorldPVS import: the module rule says server code depends on wonderland-common and wonderland-modules and does *not* import wonderland-client or lg3d-core. CellSnapshot is the memory of where furniture was, as text — one line per cell, its id then three Float.toHexString translations, so 0.1f, the float every naive %.2f format betrays, comes back bit-identical and the round trip needs no tolerance; the environment root is never written, orientation and scale survive untouched because the snapshot only claims to know *where*, a missing file is a first boot that restores 0, and a foreign or torn file is refused with an IOException before the model is touched rather than half-applied. PasscodeAuthenticator is the gate the transport was missing in front of SessionRegistry.create (which accepts whatever identity the caller hands it): a stateless HMAC-SHA256 bearer token username|hex, constant-time verified, refusal always a null and never an error that distinguishes "malformed" from "wrong signature", and the bearer-replay limitation stated in its own header rather than half-lifecycled — it is deliberately not an account system. 22 new headless cases (InterestManagerTest 7, CellSnapshotTest 7, PasscodeAuthenticatorTest 8); the fan-out of audience lists onto real sockets, the snapshot's autosave schedule and the transport wiring that calls verify() remain a running server's proof, not claimed here.
  • Bloom maths, and the post-processing ceiling stated as a decision — roadmap P3.2 (wonderland-renderer) — Java 3D 1.7.2 has no post pipeline: the fork's offscreen answer is Canvas3D render-to-image with readback, not a scene-to-texture a shader samples back, so a per-frame GPU bloom on the live 3D canvas is a missing architecture, not a missing flag. BloomKernel is the bloom as arithmetic on packed ARGB ints with nothing but java.base: a bright pass with a smoothstep knee (a raw threshold prints a ring; the knee is why this one does not), a separable box blur with clamped edges (wrap-around glows the opposite edge into the frame), and a saturating add — bloom adds light, never transparency, and strength 0 is the exact identity a future cinematic toggle will lean on. Deliberately not fast: it is the definition a faster pass gets checked against. PostProcessPlan repeats P2.2's pattern — wanting bloom is necessary but never sufficient for the live route; OFFSCREEN_READBACK opens only on a *measured* probe cost, and until then the answer is SOFTWARE_CAPTURE, blooming probe captures and the 2D desktop's composites — and the Decision carries its reason in its own words, because a silently chosen slow path gets re-litigated every release. 9 new headless cases; a glowing *live* scene stays a WlProbe sentence on a real card, which this plan refuses to decide without.
  • A follow rig and a spline tour, as frame-rate-independent maths — roadmap P3.1 (wonderland-client) — FollowRig chases a moving seat with exponential smoothing whose blend is 1 − e^(−dt/τ), so 30 fps and 300 fps produce the same lag; a gap over the teleport radius snaps instead of swim (an avatar that blinked across the map must not drag the camera through the walls), the first frame places rather than interpolates from the origin, and dt ≤ 0 freezes. Its outputs are the vocabulary the other phases already speak: eyePose(fov) is the EyeProbe.EyePose P5.3's framing kernel reads, and headingYaw() matches SpatialAudio's convention. CameraPath is a uniform Catmull-Rom through authored waypoints — passes exactly through the keys, holds the end tangents with duplicated phantoms, clamps t — and the straight-line test asserts the geometric truth a spline can actually promise (on the line, in span, the keys hit within 1e-5) rather than parameter linearity, which uniform Catmull-Rom does not have between evenly-spaced keys. 18 new headless cases (FollowRigTest 11, CameraPathTest 7); driving a live ViewerInputEngine with the rig is the walk-in's own wiring.
  • Spatial audio, with a backend that degrades when there is no device — roadmap P4.1 (wonderland-client) — audio was never ported from 2006; this phase delivers its judgement headless. SpatialAudio is the kernel: Listener/Source records, OpenAL's inverse-distance gain — whole base gain inside a source's reference distance, ref/d beyond, silent at maxDistance, and maxDistance ≤ 0 meaning no cut-off at all — and an ear-radius (0.1 m) pan model whose right vector agrees with the shadow projector's and the follow rig's yaw convention, so one heading vocabulary serves three phases. AudioManager is the WorldPVS-shaped owner: register/replace, unregister stops only what was playing, and update() returns the audible count after starting and stopping the backend. JavaSoundBackend is the first real output — one Clip per id, gain as dB (20·log₁₀, floored at −80), PAN applied only when the mixer supports it — and a machine with no audio device is a loaded silent system, not a crashed desktop: a refused LineUnavailableException on load costs that sound, nothing else. The class header says outright it is not verified by CI, because a speaker claim needs a speaker. 22 new headless cases (SpatialAudioTest 8, AudioManagerTest 10, JavaSoundBackendTest 4).
  • Shadow maths gets its projector, and the culler gets its owner — roadmap P2.4 (wonderland-renderer + wonderland-client) — ShadowProjector answers where a parallel light puts a caster's shadow pool: the pool travels the way the light travels, a low sun lengthens the run, a horizon sun caps at MAX_STRETCH instead of bandaging the campus, and a vertical or absent light answers null — which keeps the round ShadowArt blob as the physically right fallback rather than an unfinished stand-in. Box, not point, projection: the feet stay put, the top of a height-h box travels h/tan(elevation), and the pool centre sits halfway so the shadow starts *at* the caster. WorldPVS is the consultation P0.2 deliberately left unwired: cells register as they attach and unregister as they detach, a frame asks visibleFrom once, and because the kernel's contract is that registering the same id twice adds two volumes, a placement mirror rebuilt on every mutation makes a re-attached moved cell replace rather than double — bounding spheres padded by a frame of slack, conservative for drawing: a far cell may be kept, a near cell is never dropped. 13 new headless cases (ShadowProjectorTest 7, WorldPVSTest 6); re-pointing WorldScene.addShadows at the projector's yawed quad needs a live GL context and true depth occlusion remains the shadow-map upgrade — no painted pixel claimed.
  • The shader-vs-fixed decision as data, and a measured platform ceiling — roadmap P2.2 (wonderland-renderer) — ShaderAppearancePlan decides in pure data which pipeline a layered material runs on: a material with nothing beyond the diffuse layer never leaves FIXED (the pre-lit pixels survive on every platform), and an extra normal/specular layer takes SHADER only when the capability says a program would actually validate — otherwise the documented fixed-function fallback, *with the dropped layers named*, so a log says what the platform could not apply instead of the world silently looking flat. The ceiling is measured, not assumed: this repo's Jogamp fork moved the shader entry point off upstream Java 3D's Appearance.setShaderProgram onto a ShaderAppearance subclass, and a GLSL program compiles only against a live context — so J3dMeshFactory carries the decision seam and the note but not yet a program, and the GLSL 1.20 pair (one-light Blinn-Phong, tangent-space normal map, optional specular mask, P0.1 rig uniform names) ships with its sampler slots asserted to match the slots the plan binds. 7 new headless cases; attaching a program waits for a WlProbe run, and this commit claims no pixel it cannot prove.
  • Normal and specular maps have a place to live in the appearance — roadmap P2.1 (wonderland-renderer) — MaterialAppearance now carries the resolved normal- and specular-map paths beside the diffuse one (a full 12-argument constructor while the 5- and 10-arg forms delegate unchanged, and blank paths store as null), and hasNormalMap/hasSpecularMap/ layerCount() make the layer inventory headless-assertable. TextureBindingPlan.forMaterial CLASSIFIES each sampler by name — normal/bump/offset to the normal layer, spec to the specular mask — *before* its image is consulted, so the old first-present scan can no longer bind tangent-space pixels as a colour texture; a world whose only texture is named "normal" still renders exactly as before, through the double-duty binding. The layers are inert until P2.2's path applies them — the fixed pipeline has no normal-map slot — and this claims no pixel. 31 headless cases (MaterialAppearanceTest 11, TextureBindingPlanTest 20).
  • The eye probe, formalised — roadmap P5.3 (wonderland-client + lg3d-apps) — every visual phase defers to "verified by the eye probe", which is true but not CI. EyeProbe is the framing kernel, pure: given an EyePose (position, look direction, field of view) and each cell's bounding sphere it decides in-frame vs out with a dot-product + angle test, generous at the edge so a sliver is never dropped and safe on the degenerate cases (target at the eye, zero-length look); frame() returns the whole verdict as ordered data, no Java 3D and no display involved. ProbeHarness hands that verdict to a Mandela probe script as bound scalars — in-frame/off-frame id lists, counts, fov, eye position — and reads back the script's value under exactly WorldBehavior's fail-safe contract, so a broken or absent probe is a missing report, never a throw onto a caller. Together they make a later rig or renderer change assertable in CI ("after the rig turns, exactly these cells are in frame"); the scripting half stays in lg3d-apps because Mandela must not enter wonderland-client. 14 new headless cases (EyeProbeTest 8, ProbeHarnessTest 6); painted pixels remain the live capture's proof.
  • The clinic ships its first real behaviour script — roadmap P5.2 (wonderland-server resources + lg3d-apps) — P5.1 gave every walk-in world a behaviour hook; this ships the first one worth reading. The outpatient clinic's behaviour.mnd sits beside its art (wonderland-outpatient-clinic/behaviour.mnd) and the walk-in reads it through the same /api/world/asset endpoint the models already use — no new server code. The script refines each cell the way its own class says it should: a seeded AvatarCell becomes "a visitor", a pinned picture "a notice on the wall", a model cell "the *label*" (its height noted when it rises over the floor slab), and anything else keeps the label its author wrote; it binds only host-supplied cell facts and holds no scene-graph handle, so it can only ever annotate a cell, never invent or erase one. ClinicBehaviourTest (6 cases) reads the shipped file by repository path and pins what each kind of cell becomes, including that an unplaced cell degrades to its own label rather than a crash. The script deliberately does *not* live under scripts/mandela/ — those are self-contained programs compiled without host bindings — so this test, not ShippedScriptsTest, is its gate.
  • The scene goes physical: PVS culling, real collision, trigger zones — roadmap P0.2 / P1.1 / P1.2 (wonderland-client) — three headless pure kernels, each the object the renderer will one day drive, proven in CI with no display and no Java 3D import. OctantCuller is a regular-grid spatial hash over cell bounding spheres: register/query(eye, radius) walk only the buckets a sight sphere touches and return a PotentialVisibleSet carrying a cullRatio, so "a culler that returns everything" is a failing assertion rather than a silent win — and the answer is *provably independent of bucket size*, asserted, so cellSize is only ever a work knob (11 cases). Collision existed only as a (height, boolean) message with no decider behind it, so the walker went wherever it asked: Obstacle is decision-made data (an AABB plus a height band), WalkerCollision the pure walk-step resolver, and AvatarCollider the stateful adapter ViewCell.localMoveRequest now uses — one that SWEPTS each axis instead of point-testing the endpoint, so a fast step cannot tunnel through a thin wall by landing on its far side — and when two walls share one lane, the wall that stops the walker is the one met FIRST: the near face wins, whichever order the world registered its obstacles in. That near-face rule is itself a defect found and fixed while pinning the sweep's branches — a single-wall test could never have disproved the swept lane choosing the farthest stopping face. The collider is an optional collaborator: unset, it forwards the move untouched, and a world that has not authored collision behaves byte-for-byte as before (32 cases). TriggerZone (a footprint plus an optional height band) and TriggerField remember the inside-set and emit only membership *edges* per move — once per crossing, silent while loitering — returned as a value its host decides what to do with (9 cases). No new server code, no new wire format. 52 new headless cases across five suites.
  • Mandela cell behaviours for Wonderland — roadmap P5.1 (lg3d-apps) — a world can now have one opinion about its own cells without a rebuild: it ships a single behaviour.mnd beside its art, and the walk-in renderer reads it through the same cached world store (and the same asset endpoint the models already use). WorldBehavior binds each model cell's plain facts — label, name, cellType, position, footprint, and whether it is a model, an avatar or a picture, with a missing number bound as 0.0 so script arithmetic never trips — runs the script through Mandela.eval(source, Map), and reads back exactly one thing: an annotation floating over that cell. A script never sees the scene graph and the bridge never throws onto the render path — a null, blank, throwing or empty-valued behaviour, and one the world simply does not ship, all collapse to the label the cell was authored with, so every bundled world renders exactly as it did before the feature existed. 14 new headless cases (WorldBehaviorTest) prove the decision and the safety without a display; showing an annotation on a live cell remains the walk-in probe's job, the same division the lighting rig above accepted for its shading. Grounded in docs/wonderland-roadmap.md.
  • Opt-in lighting for the renderer, and the Wonderland 3D roadmap (wonderland-renderer + docs) — docs/wonderland-roadmap.md now records what the port actually carries (multiplayer and sessions are *real*; collision is a message stub; audio was never ported) and phases the work forward. Its first step is honest about the renderer's load-bearing constraint, proved by build-gradle/scratch/WlProbe7: the shipped COLLADA art is pre-lit, so a Material is deliberately absent and turning Java 3D lighting on over it dims every surface to ~18 % of its authored colour. So lighting is additive, never global: MaterialAppearance gained an opt-in shading model (lit plus ambient/specular/emissive/shininess, each falling back to a sane value and defensively copied), J3dMeshFactory builds a Java 3D Material — and a MODULATE texture — only when a material asks to be lit, and WorldScene gained a pure Lighting value and a build(entries, pictures, lighting) overload that installs an AmbientLight + DirectionalLight scoped to the world. A Light changes nothing for an Appearance with no Material, so the two-argument build (which passes Lighting.NONE) renders a pre-lit world byte-identically to before, and the whole lighting *decision* lives in pure values that need no native stack: 12 new headless cases (7 MaterialAppearanceTest — the unlit default, the round-tripped channels, the defensive copy, the null/short/negative fallbacks — and 5 Lighting in WorldSceneTest — NONE disabled, colour/direction round-trip, non-unit and zero-length suns normalised, a NaN colour replaced). What is *not* verified here is the on-screen shading itself: a Material/Light needs a live render context, so the raster is left to the WorldViewer display probe rather than claimed green.
  • A walk-in that talks: text chat on the cell channel (wonderland-common + wonderland-server + wonderland-client) — the ported wire carries moves, seats and views, and nothing else, so two visitors in the same room were two people who could not acknowledge each other. TextChatMessage is a CellMessage, and that choice is the port's constraint rather than a style: CellChannelConnection demultiplexes inbound traffic by CellID and casts every frame to CellMessage without checking, so a session-level message has no channel to land on without cutting a new seam into a verbatim-ported class. The address is the world's environment cell — the one cell the server's SET_VIEW fan-out guarantees every session has loaded — and the server refuses any other, rather than relaying to a cell whose listeners happen to include the sender. Two things stay the server's to decide: the sender's *name*, rewritten from the authenticated identity so a client cannot speak for somebody else, and the *bounds*, re-validated by constructing the relayed copy (Java serialisation runs no constructor, so a hand-made frame can arrive with a null or enormous body). The author's own line comes back around the relay like anyone else's, which is why there is exactly one transcript and it is the server's. ChatChannel is the client half — transport only, no model — and the transcript stays where it belongs, in ChatConversation. 27 new headless cases: 2 in CellMessagesCodecTest (the message survives the packer, and an oversized body is refused at construction), 4 in ProtocolRouterTest (relay to peers, name rewrite, wrong-address refusal, malformed body answered as an ErrorMessage rather than a stack trace on the transport thread) and 21 in ChatChannelTest (install on cell load, tear down on unload, send with the placeholder name, deliver to listeners, never throw at a dead session).
  • The walk-in window gains a sidebar, and the world stops stealing the keyboard (wonderland-renderer + lg3d-apps) — the reference photograph of this world is not a picture of geometry: it shows a *Users (9)* roster and a chat box on the room, so an Enter World window with neither was a clinic that had been evacuated. WorldViewer.setSidebar(Component) docks any panel on the frame's east side and works before or after show(), taking the width back from the canvas when the panel arrives. On top of it, WorldVisit opens the other half of a session — the same three /comms sockets and the same CellClientSession the 3D desktop uses — and folds what they carry into WorldVisitPanel: the roster is the set of *foreign view cells the server said exist* (ProtocolRouter mints one per SET_VIEW and pushes it to everyone else; a depart arrives as cellUnloaded), not a list this client invents, and the transcript is ChatChannel on the same session. What it honestly does not claim is another visitor's *body* in the scene — the walk-in's canvas is a Java 3D graph built from a REST read, and mounting a live cell into it is separate work — so a roster of three with two empty chairs is the current state, and the strip says "here" rather than "standing in front of you". The one line this had to add to the viewer is a guard: AWT forwards a frame's children's unconsumed KEY_PRESSED events, so typing "water" into a chat field walked the eye west five times. keyboardIsForTheWorld() now lets a keystroke reach the walker only when the frame, the canvas or the sidebar itself holds focus, and never when a text field does — W A S D Q E are letters before they are commands. 18 new headless cases (WorldVisitTest, WorldVisitPanelTest) drive the panel from a fake session and assert the roster by reading the model back.
  • The clinic's hall is furnished: six wall cards, authored as GUI cells (wonderland-server) — the 2009 view is a *room*, and the ported hall was an empty box: the reference's health notice board, its two windows and its three framed prints existed nowhere in the world. They arrive as <poster-cell> GUI cells rather than as models, which is what the format's own picture cell carries — a name, a wla:// image and a measure in pixel scale, with no .dae, no .dep and no lighting to author — and the difference is not styling: hung as a model cell, each one would also arrive *signed*, because the renderer reads any cell over 0.6 m tall as a room and puts its name near the ceiling, and a notice board does not need a name when it is already covered in one. Three maps carry the art (art/): notices.png is the four-quadrant board (Health / Clinic Hours / Wash Hands / Exam Room) at 512 px and 3.4 mm per pixel, which is the 1.74 m board a person reads from three metres; picture.png is the 0.9 m framed print at 3.5 mm, small on purpose — a wall-sized version of the same image is a mural, which is a different thing to have paid for; and glass.png is the window pane. The hall goes from 18 cells to 24, with no Java change and no new model. Two gates hold it: the server's REST surface now publishes the six cards with their type, asset and measure, and WorldCatalogTest.everyWallArtCardClearsThePlasterItHangsOn() walks every wall-art card and asserts it stands 10–30 cm off the wall it illustrates — the hall's inner faces measured off clinic-room.dae's own vertices (|x| = 11.0, |z| = 8.0) rather than off the .dep bounding box, whose 0.506 is the outer edge of the wall's *thickness*. A card hung at 11.0 exactly is hung inside the wall it shows, and the wall wins the depth test.
  • The world browser can now start the world it shows — and shows what it starts (wonderland-server + lg3d-apps) — the picker listed every catalog world, but Start Server against a stale or foreign server already answering on the port did nothing: ensureRunning found the port busy, "already answers" won, the chosen world was never seeded, and Stop Server rightly refused to kill a process it did not own; and in the 2D desktop there was no viewer at all, so a world had no face beyond its cell rows. Two new server-side facts close that loop. WorldModel now remembers its liveModule — set only when seeding succeeds — and GET /api/world/worlds marks exactly that entry hosted: true, so "is *my* world running" is one read, not a guess; and GET /api/world/cells?module= describes each cell's authored placement — the position component's translation as x/y/z and its bounds as width/depth (stored half-extents, doubled on read) — purely additive fields an older reader ignores. The client WorldCatalog parses both, and a missing or non-positive footprint stays null, because "nowhere" and "at the origin" must not read as the same number. The launcher's contract is now honest: a server that answers *and hosts the chosen world* is left exactly as its owner started it; one that does not (the stale case — the old jar cannot even answer the hosting question) is walked past, and the panel's own seeded server starts on the next free localhost port (a bounded scan) with Result.url carrying the new address, which Start Server then writes back into the server field so every later read follows the server the press actually brought up; a remote server is still never touched. And the vignette, which is the half the picker was missing: the original Wonderland browser answered "what does this world look like?" with a *picture*, so the server now serves one — GET /api/world/preview?module= hands back the world's own preview.png (.jpg/.jpeg too, and the art/ spelling the world jars already use) from the very store the models come from, and answers a plain 404 when a world ships none; WorldPreviewPanel paints that picture aspect-kept above the cell tree and falls back to a floor plan only when there is no picture to show. The plan is WorldPlan (pure, headless) folding a world's placed cells into the unit square — one uniform scale so aspect survives, +z up, the environment root and unplaced cells skipped, a missing footprint drawn as a unit square, a degenerate all-in-one-point world inflated instead of dividing by zero — plus the two rules that turned an unreadable cluster into a map: the one cell covering 3/4 of the world on both axes is the *ground*, so it frames the plan instead of setting its scale (the clinic's 48×36 Floor had been shrinking its nine rooms to specks, and their names to mush), and a label is wrapped into its own box or left out, never painted over its neighbours. Stock-world art is wired only where it is true: of the seven shipped world jars exactly one image is a rendered view of a world — art/Japanese-Pavilion-portal3.png, which pictures the pavilion while sitting in the combined jar — so the pavilion borrows it by name and the other six worlds get the plan; the library's other poster-shaped asset, OWLDefaultWorldPoster.v2-sm.png, is a text signboard reading "Use the Placemarks menu to explore this world", and serving it as a preview would lie about what the world looks like. 12 new headless cases on the server (liveModule's set-and-blank-clears contract, a seeded world recording the module it hosts, hosted marking only the seeded module, a module's cells carrying the authored placement, the bundled clinic's describeCells case now asserting Exam Room 1's authored −8/−5 spot and its doubled 8×8 footprint, the preview resolve order — a module's own preview.png, then its art/ spelling, then the alias — and the endpoint's 200-with-the-right-media-type and 404-when-none) and 30 on the desktop side (port rewriting that keeps everything but the port, a hosted server left alone, relocation past a foreign unseeded server, the every-nearby-port-taken admission, the panel following a relocated server, the picture painted when the server has one and the plan when it does not, an absent, undecodable or unreachable preview costing the world read nothing, both cleared on a failed read, twelve WorldPlan normalization and ground rules, and the hosted/geometry/preview parse). All verified live: with a stale jar holding 8080, the real panel's Start Server spawned seeded servers on 8081 and 8082 instead of giving up; a fresh jar's /api/world/worlds marks only the clinic hosted; and /api/world/cells?module=wonderland-outpatient-clinic returned all nine named rooms with their authored placement (Exam Room 1 at x=−8 z=−5, 8×8; the Floor 48×36), the stock wonderland-town-world jar likewise.
  • The Wonderland client session went production: the world is now seen, not just listed (wonderland-client + lg3d-apps) — the port had no real WonderlandSession past the in-JVM loopback, so the 3D world frame opened empty: every HUD row stayed PENDING and nothing ever called cellLoaded. WebSocketWonderlandSession now speaks the server's /comms binary wire directly: every frame is one MessagePacker envelope, each channel's first attach mints or rejoins the server session (the follow-on sockets echo it under wonderland.sessionID, hex, so the three channel/cache/edit sockets converge on one ServerSession), and the short the AttachedClientMessage assigned stamps every later frame. The java.net.http.WebSocket transport sits behind a Transport/TransportFactory seam, so the whole handshake, fan-out and every failure path is headless-tested (26 cases, including one real RFC 6455 round trip against a miniature server). WonderlandWorld3D, the 3D desktop's start-menu command, walks in over it: a daemon thread connects a CellClientSession to the panel's server as the desktop's own user, and the cache listener is registered *before* the connect because the server's view-cell flush begins with the SET_VIEW handshake itself — each cellLoaded mounts its renderer through WonderlandDesktop / CellFrameBridge, each cellUnloaded takes it back out, and closing the HUD disconnects the session before unmounting the world. And Start Server now seeds the world the picker holds (--wonderland.world.seed=<module>, defaulting to the bundled clinic; a server that already answers is left exactly as its owner started it) — a server hosting nothing would show an empty Environment even to a perfect client. Verified live: a bare CellCacheConnection over the production session against a java -jar server seeded with wonderland-outpatient-clinic received the Environment root, all nine clinic cells and its own view cell over the sockets.
  • The Wonderland World browser became a world picker with Start/Stop server control (wonderland-server + lg3d-apps) — the panel was a reader of the one world a server happened to seed: it dumped GET /api/world/cells and, when nothing answered, dead-ended on a bare "cannot reach". It now does what the catalog endpoint always made possible. GET /api/world/cells?module= reads any catalog world's cells on demand (WorldCatalog.describeCells loads the module through the same store the seeder would pick and classifies each cell exactly as seeding would — a model cell as the renderer class, every other named cell as the environment root — so the browser listing a world can never disagree with what hosting it would show; a module's cells are siblings, so every parent is null, and an unknown or unopenable world yields an empty list, never a 500). On the desktop side WorldCatalog learned to read /api/world/worlds (loadWorlds/parseWorlds → WorldEntry) and to ask for one world's cells (loadWorld), and WonderlandWorldPanel gained a world dropdown over the server host/port field: it lists every available world, opens the first (or whichever you pick), and shows that world's cells. Spring Boot is operated from the panel: a Start Server button brings a local wonderland-server up on the field's address and reads its catalog when the press lands, a Stop Server button reaps the child the panel started (and honestly refuses to touch a server it does not own), and a failed read at a local address also starts the server itself — WonderlandServerLauncher finds the bootJar the build already produced (wonderland-server/build-gradle/libs/*-app.jar, overridable by lg.wonderland.server.jar, and found by walking up from the working directory or the desktop's own code location, so a :lg3d-core:run desktop started inside the module still finds it), passes it --wonderland.world.dir when extractWorlds has unpacked the stock world jars beside the build (without the flag the server sees only the bundled classpath clinic), spawns java -jar on the field's port, and polls readiness before reloading the catalog; it only ever touches a *localhost* address (a remote server is somebody else's process), it never throws, and on any failure the panel falls back to the same manual bootRun hint it showed before, so auto-start is a convenience rather than a new dependency the browser can hang on. Verified live against the freshly built jar: /api/world/cells?module=wonderland-outpatient-clinic returns the nine clinic cells from an unseeded server, and the panel's first refresh now lists and opens a world instead of an empty error strip.
  • Wonderland server became startable (wonderland-server, gradle, root build.gradle) — the module's application.properties documented bootRun, SERVER_PORT and -Dserver.port, but the Spring Boot Gradle plugin was never applied, so those entry points did not exist: the @SpringBootTest suite boots Tomcat in-JVM and never revealed the gap, and there was no way for a human to actually run the server. Applying the plugin (version managed once in the root plugins block as apply false) adds bootRun and an executable bootJar; the plain library jar is kept under its bare, expected name (what CI and any consumer resolve) with the fat jar alongside it under the -app classifier.
  • The Wonderland server can host a world — the outpatient clinic seeds (wonderland-server + wonderland-modules) — M5 built the world pipeline (WorldLoader decodes a module's *-wlc.xml cells and resolves their wla:// deployed models headless) and M6c2 built the render bridge, but nothing ever fed one into the other: a running server hosted only the Environment root, so /api/world/cells — the very endpoint the desktop's Wonderland World browser reads — listed nothing to walk. WorldSeeder closes that last mile on the server side: at boot it loads a named world module through a new ManifestClasspathWorldStore and, for each decoded cell, mints a CellID and stores a WorldCell carrying the renderer class name (inert string data, so the server still never imports the renderer), the human name, and the transform lifted from the position component. Enumeration needed an index the plain ClasspathWorldStore deliberately refuses to provide (a jar cannot be walked across exploded and packaged layouts), so the new store reads <module>/world-index.txt and answers listAssets from it while every other operation delegates to the classpath store's confinement rule. Seeding is opt-in and off by default (wonderland.world.seed=none): the M3b socket integration test asserts an empty world fans out exactly the environment plus the fresh view, and a world that cannot load degrades to an empty server with a warning rather than a boot failure — a bad world must never stop a server. The shipped content is a clean-room outpatient clinic, recreating the community "TMS Medical Center" world from outpatientclinic.jpg: nine named cells (Floor, Reception, Clinic Directory, Exam Room 1 + Waiting, Exam Room 2 + Waiting, Patient Education, Observation Room) resolved through one reusable unit-box deployed model. wonderland-server gained the wonderland-modules dependency, and the Spring Boot BOM's JAXB 4.x (which renamed the packages to jakarta.xml.bind) is pinned back to the 2.3.x line the ported javax.xml.bind cell-state code needs — safe because the server speaks JSON REST and a binary WebSocket, nothing consumes the jakarta.xml.bind namespace. 12 new headless cases (6 in WorldSeederTest proving the off-by-default, seed-every-named- cell, model/non-model class assignment, transform lift, and never-throw contracts against synthetic states; 6 in ManifestClasspathWorldStoreTest proving manifest discovery, comment/blank filtering, suffix match, sort, the absent-index degrade and a corrupt-stream degrade against real test resources), plus a wonderland-indexed-world fixture. Verified live, not just in CI: bootRun --args='--wonderland.world.seed=wonderland-outpatient-clinic' makes /api/world/cells return the environment plus all nine clinic cells. What this does not yet claim is the 3D walk: rendering those cells needs the production WebSocket WonderlandSession and asset HTTP serving that are the next increment, so this entry proves the server hosts the world, not that a room was seen on screen.
  • Access to every existing Wonderland world, plus the world-library agent guide (wonderland-server + wonderland-modules + wonderland-server/AGENTS.md) — the server could seed the one bundled clinic; it could not see, let alone host, the seven stock Open Wonderland worlds (almostempty, auditorium, combined, gallery, japanesepavilion, meetingcomplex, town) that ship as packaged wonderland-*-world.jar modules inside the gitignored 400 MB installer. They are made reachable without committing a single binary. JarWorldStore (wonderland-modules) reads a world module jar directly: a JarFile *is* enumerable, so listAssets walks its entries — the very enumeration the classpath store refuses — and open/present try the module-root entry then the art/ sibling, because each stock world spells its art as wla://<module>/<path> at the module root while the jar packs those bytes under art/; the mismatch is bridged on read, so no vendored binary is ever rewritten. WorldCatalog (wonderland-server) merges the two origins — bundled classpath worlds (always offered) and installed *-world.jars in the new wonderland.world.dir directory — into a WorldSummary per world (module, title and description read from module.xml, source, cellCount), every read defensive so one bad jar hides neither the rest nor the boot. The WorldSeeder now selects a JarWorldStore when the seed names an installed jar, else the classpath store, keeping the opt-in/never-throw contract. GET /api/world/worlds serves the catalog, read independently of the seeded world so a browser lists what is available before any world loads. :wonderland-server:extractWorlds unpacks the seven stock jars from the local installer into a gitignored wonderland-worlds/ (it warns and succeeds when no installer is present, so it is never a build dependency and is not wired into check). 13 new headless cases (5 in JarWorldStoreTest building a synthetic world jar in a @TempDir to prove enumeration, the art/ read fallback, exact-match preference and the absent-asset degrade; 6 in WorldCatalogTest proving bundled/jar discovery, the corrupt-jar and missing-module.xml degrades and the unconfigured-directory cases; 2 in WorldSeederTest seeding from a jar and skipping an unnamed cell) plus a /worlds case in WorldRestControllerTest. Verified live: extractWorlds then bootRun --args='--wonderland.world.dir=wonderland-worlds --wonderland.world.seed=wonderland-town-world' returns all eight worlds from /api/world/worlds (clinic source classpath/9 cells, combined-world 41, meetingcomplex-world 11, …) and fans out the seeded town world's cells. wonderland-server/AGENTS.md is the new role guide — it teaches world authoring (the clinic as the worked module, module.xml/*-wlc.xml/wla:// chain, the world-index.txt a classpath world needs and the BUNDLED registration) and world access (extraction, the directory knob, the catalog endpoint), and is indexed from the root AGENTS.md module table.
  • The world's art is served over HTTP — the first Stage-2 walk pieces (wonderland-server) — the world library could list and seed cells, but a cell named its model only as a wla:// reference the renderer had no way to fetch, so nothing downstream could actually load a room. Two isolated, safe pieces close that over plain HTTP while the shared wire format stays untouched. WorldSeeder now captures each model cell's wla://<module>/<path> deployed-model URL from the decoded ModelCellComponentServerState and stores it on the WorldCell (a new immutable field, defaulted null so the existing 7-arg form and every caller is unchanged), and GET /api/world/cells puts it in the descriptor only for a cell that carries one — the environment root's JSON is byte-for-byte what it was. WorldCatalog.openAssetBytes resolves one asset's bytes from whichever store backs the module (the classpath for a bundled world, its jar for an installed one), reading and closing the jar per call so no file handle outlives a request and degrading to empty on any miss rather than throwing; GET /api/world/asset?module=&path= serves those bytes, rejecting a path that escapes the module root (.., leading /, backslash) as a 400 before the store is consulted, and an absent asset as a 404 — a broken reference is never a 500. Deliberately server-side and HTTP only: folding the URL into ModelCellClientState would be the shared-wire-format change this stage defers (there is no loadable client model component yet), so a walk host can enumerate /cells and pull each cell's whole model chain over /asset with no socket change. 11 new headless cases (3 in WorldSeederTest proving the URL is captured on a model cell and absent on a non-model one; 4 in WorldRestControllerTest proving the descriptor URL, a jar asset's bytes, the real bundled clinic module.xml served over the classpath branch, the 404 and the 400; 3 in WorldCatalogTest on openAssetBytes) plus the classpath/jar resolution seams. Verified live: seeding the clinic fills deployedModelURL on all nine model cells, and /api/world/asset returns the referenced clinic-box.dep (1046 B) and clinic-box.dae (2357 B) as 200, a missing path as 404 and a ../ traversal as 400.
  • The model URL now crosses the shared wire format — Stage 2 complete (wonderland-common + wonderland-renderer + wonderland-server) — the safe pieces above kept the wla:// reference server-side, reachable only over HTTP; a native client walking in over the socket still received a bare CellClientState and could not learn which model to render. That deferral is now closed on purpose. ModelCellClientState, an empty name-only stub, gains a deployedModelURL field (plain Serializable state on the existing wire type, with an explicit serialVersionUID so a future field is a conscious wire change, not a silent deserialisation break); WorldSeeder folds a model cell's captured URL into a ModelCellClientState carried as the cell's client state, so the LOAD_CELL message the router pushes delivers it to a client, while the WorldCell field stays the HTTP-descriptor copy — one URL, two surfaces on purpose. On the receiving side the renderer's WonderlandModelCell gains the (CellID, CellCache) constructor the client cache reflects open by class name and a setClientState override that reads the URL back — exactly the "ModelCellClientState carrying a wla:// reference" design its own file header described, now wired end to end; a null URL leaves any loader-supplied value in place. 7 new headless cases (2 in CellMessagesCodecTest proving the URL survives Java serialisation inside both a CellClientStateMessage and the real CellHierarchyMessage LOAD_CELL setup data; 2 in WorldSeederTest proving a model cell's client state is a ModelCellClientState with the URL and a non-model cell keeps a plain state; 3 in WonderlandModelCellTest on the cache constructor and the setClientState read plus its two null guards) on top of the existing suite, and the in-JVM LoopbackClientServerTest (everyHopRodeTheRealCodec) still passes — proof the new client state packs and unpacks over the real codec, not an object reference. Verified live: seeding the clinic still fills deployedModelURL on all nine model cells over /api/world/cells and /api/world/asset still serves them (200/400/404), so the wire change is additive to the HTTP surface, not a regression of it. What this still does not claim is an on-screen 3D room: rendering needs a live Java 3D canvas and the production WebSocket WonderlandSession, and the server test classpath deliberately never imports the renderer (the class name stays inert data), so the walk's visual half remains the next, separate surface.
  • Mandela got a version of its own (lg3d-mandela, gradle.properties, scripts/mandela) — the language module carried the desktop's 1.69.0-dev as its own identity while its real version was two hard-coded "1.0" strings nobody compared to anything, so a host that embedded the jar could not ask which language it had been given and mandela --version answered from memory. A module that depends on nothing releases on its own clock, and counting it in desktop versions says nothing about it: mandela.version (the jar, now 1.0.0) and mandela.language (the grammar, 1.0) in gradle.properties are the authority, the build overrides the module's version from them and stamps both into the jar manifest (Implementation-Version, Specification-Version), Mandela.IMPLEMENTATION_VERSION reads 1.0.0, and the module's own CHANGELOG.md — nine lines, a header with two typos in it and no entries at all — now carries the version policy and the release's record. The copies are what drift, so mandela-version.mnd joins the gates and compares the eight places the two numbers are written against their property; the jar name three of those documents quoted had gone stale at 1.68.0-dev while the build said 1.69.0-dev, so the module's docs now spell it lg3d-mandela-<version>.jar and only the two invocations the gate reads still name a number. The desktop's release train never rewrites Mandela's version and release-check.mnd does not look at it — the bundle puts the jar on a lib/* wildcard classpath, which does not care what the file is called — so a Mandela bump is its own module-scoped chore, gated by its own script.
  • Mandela 1.1.0: the roadmap's next horizon landed whole (lg3d-mandela, scripts/mandela, docs/mandela-language.md) — the gates in scripts/mandela/ each hand-rolled the same scans (an indexOf-loop occurrence count, a first-pair key=value split, a trim-to-empty test, a filter-then-refilter split), and the browser host held a private */? matcher no script could reach, so the language grew what its own automation was repeating: string members count, splitOnce, isBlank, removePrefix/removeSuffix, lines and words; list members count (bare, or with a predicate) and partition; and std.glob — matches(text, pattern) / isMatch(pattern, text), a segment-scan matcher that never backtracks, which is why a glob fits the step-budget sandbox while a regular expression never will (guide §12 still says no regex; §9 now shows what to use instead). Two scripts ship with it: changelog-check.mnd, the tenth repository gate, proves CHANGELOG.md keeps the shape its three readers — help topic, Pages archive, Update Manager — all parse, and todo-scan.mnd is a report (always exit 0) inventorying the tree's open TODO/FIXME markers. The grammar is untouched, so this is a jar bump alone: mandela.version 1.0.0 → 1.1.0 with mandela.language still 1.0, every copy kept in step by mandela-version.mnd, recorded in lg3d-mandela/CHANGELOG.md.
  • A release is now a page, and the page carries its test reports (scripts/mandela + documentation/ + .github/workflows/) — the changelog had always been rendered for one audience only: whats-new.mnd parsed CHANGELOG.md into the Help Center's What's New topic and stopped there, so a release's notes were readable on the desktop or on GitHub but never on the documentation site, and the reports CI generates (under <module>/build-gradle/reports/) vanished with the run that made them. The script now parses once and renders twice: the help topic, byte for byte unchanged, and one page per released version under documentation/releases/ plus an index.html listing them, in the site's own skin, with the portal's bilingual cards (documentation/index.html) pointing at that index so no page is reachable only by a deep link. Eight pages and the index are committed — every ## [ header of CHANGELOG.md except [Unreleased], at this writing — because a committed page is a page the gates can check: whatsNewCheck no longer compares one file, it byte-compares the topic *and* every archive page, and reports a missing page, a stale page or a page whose version has left the changelog as findings carrying the one instruction that fixes them; htmlLinksCheck audits their links like any other page of the site. Test reports are never committed, for the reason the Javadoc is not: a committed copy rots on the next test run. .github/workflows/release-reports.yml runs on a published Release (or a manual run on an existing tag), rebuilds test, jacocoTestReport, jacocoTestCoverageVerification, :lg3d-mandela:pitest and :lg3d-mandela:repositoryChecks from the tagged source, stages releases/<version>/reports/{junit,jacoco,cucumber,pitest}/, publishes the version's page beside that tree, pushes the result append-only onto a site-releases storage branch and attaches the same tree to the Release as reports-<version>.zip, then asks deploy-docs.yml — still the only publisher of Pages — to run, which overlays the branch while it deploys. The link between a committed page and an uncommitted tree is a placeholder: the page carries a <!-- test-reports --> comment the workflow substitutes with links into the tree it just built, because a committed href into a directory that exists only after CI would be a dead link in every checkout, and htmlLinksCheck would rightly refuse the pull request. The page says what the reports are instead of flattering the release: PIT covers lg3d-mandela, the only module the repository configures it for, so the figure is the language core and the page calls it that. A tag with no archive page (a development or pre-release build) still gets its zip, and the site simply does not gain a page. The gate was proven to bite — removing one archive page turns :lg3d-mandela:whatsNewCheck red naming the count — before the pages shipped green, and the Javadoc remains off Pages behind the existing guard in deploy-docs.yml.
  • Wonderland reaches the desktop — the M6c2 integration, in 2D and 3D (wonderland-desktop + lg3d-apps + lg3d-core) — the milestone this port had been reporting as "awaits re-confirmation" while M7 shipped on top of it, and the audit that reopened the milestone found real missing functionality in two directions. On the scene graph, WonderlandWorldContainer stops being a mount that only remembers: each cell now gets its own BranchGroup → pose TransformGroup → visibility Switch → renderer-scene chain under the container's Java3DGraph child, so setVisible — the documented no-op M6c1 left — is a real Switch.CHILD_ALL / CHILD_NONE edit, gating in the container rather than in the renderer so the shell can hide a cell without touching the client's own DISK→VISIBLE status, and addJ3dChild's PickTool.setCapabilities(node, INTERSECT_COORD) walk is what makes a cell pickable at all; a node→cellId identity map registered before the branch goes live answers "which cell owns this hit" without a parent walk. The decision layers are pure and headless: SessionFeed folds the client's cellLoaded / cellUnloaded / cellTransformUpdate stream into bridge calls, PickRouter + PickDecision + PickIntent make the routing answer (nearest mounted cell wins, a cell that is not mounted cannot be picked, and a gesture the world does not claim — the wheel above all — stays with the desktop's scene manager), WorldInputRouter adapts lg3d's picked MouseEvent3D vocabulary to that decision and never lets a failure escape onto the desktop's event thread, and WorldInventory + WorldHudModel compute the HUD snapshot (depth-first rows over the parent links with a seeded seen-set, MOUNTED / HIDDEN / PENDING per cell, the one-line summary). The Swing and launcher half follows the repository's app-layer convention and lives in lg3d-apps, mirroring the update-manager / db-manager pattern: WorldCatalog reads the M3 server's own /api/world/cells REST view with the JDK HTTP client + Jackson (one truth about the world, never a second one compiled by hand), WonderlandWorldPanel is the read-only browser hosted both ways — a 2D MDI JInternalFrame through Desktop2DAppRegistry.PANEL_APPS and a 3D SwingNode through TitledSwingWindow — WorldCatalogInventory adapts that catalog to the bridge's WorldInventory instead of duplicating an HTTP stack inside it, WonderlandHudPanel is the mount HUD writing Show / Hide through the bridge, and WonderlandWorld3D is the in-JVM launcher that installs the renderer, hands the world to the scene manager as a Frame3D and opens the HUD. Two .lgcfg start-menu descriptors and their generated icons (wonderland.png, wonderland3d.png, both from GenerateAppIcons) put them on the menu; WonderlandWorld3D is deliberately absent from Desktop2DAppRegistry, so the 2D shell classifies it UNAVAILABLE and drops it rather than building a scene graph with no universe to hold it, while the read-only browser stays available in both desktops. 109 new headless cases (61 in wonderland-desktop, taking the module from 27 to 88 — CellFrameBridgeTest +7, SessionFeedTest 13, PickRouterTest 17, WorldHudModelTest 16, WorldInputRouterTest 8; 48 in lg3d-apps — WorldCatalogTest 22, WonderlandHudPanelTest 11, WonderlandWorldPanelTest 10, WorldCatalogInventoryTest 5), plus two assertions in Desktop2DAppRegistryTest; coverageFloors[wonderland-desktop] rises [0.410, 0.540] → [0.610, 0.710] (measured 61.90 % / 71.36 %, the residue still exactly the probe-only Component3D / bootstrap classes). No rendering is claimed from CI: live mounting remains verified by the in-JVM desktop probe + the lgscreen-0-N.png screencapture, and this entry claims the path exists, not that a world was seen on screen.
  • The Wonderland VoIP softphone lands on ice4j + Java Sound + in-tree G.711 (wonderland-modules + lg3d-apps, M7d) — the fourth and last M7 replacement, and the one that was three dead technologies braided together: the 2006 phone bundled a closed SIP binary driven over a stdin/stdout line protocol, watched it with winp (native JNI, Windows-only, retired), looked up its NAT reflexive address with stun.jar (never open-sourced), and carried voice through JMF RTP (javax.media, unrecoverable). The port splits the same job along the M4 headless line: wonderland-modules/softphone is a dependency-free package — SoftphoneControl (the 2006 SoftphoneControlImpl's STATE half ported method-for-method: call id, mute, visibility, quality, recorder rules, listener fan-out, and the exitNotificationSent "fire softphoneExited AT MOST ONCE per process" rule kept verbatim in spirit), SoftphoneCommand / SoftphoneEvent (the SAME line vocabulary the 2006 binary spoke — "register", "callID=", "mute"/ "Unmute", "quality", "recordAudio=", "linetest", "PlaceCall=…", "Shutdown", and the stdout echoes — now typed, serialised and parsed, so a modern host softphone is scripted against the identical protocol), RtpPacket (the RFC 3550 fixed header as an immutable value class — V|P|X|CC and M|PT in their spec octets, the modulo-2^16 sequence circle, and refusals for what the 2006 stack never spoke), G711 (the public-domain mu-law quantiser from Sun's g711.c in pure Java, exhaustively tested: all 65536 shorts encode, all 256 codes decode, the round trip lands within one quantisation step, the two ISDN zeros expand to silence), JitterBuffer (the TreeMap de-jitter reorder on extended sequence positions with its capacity, gap and late-drop counters), VuMeter (the peak-follower needle that emits the 2006 "Microphone level: N%" strings and latches the gain warning), AudioQuality (the four 2006 presets value-for-value), the listener triad, SoftphoneBackend + NoopSoftphoneBackend + the SoftphonePlugin.installBackendFactory seam — the eighth shipped ServiceLoader provider. The live half is lg3d-apps: an ExternalSoftphoneBackend spawns and supervises the child with ProcessBuilder + java.lang.ProcessHandle (the winp replacement — its protocol framing is headless-tested against an in-memory EngineProcess stub), an Ice4jNatProbe asks ice4j (Apache-2.0, the Jitsi engine on Maven Central) the same "where is my public address behind this NAT" question stun.jar asked (probe-only — a fabricated STUN server would prove nothing), and a JavaSoundVoiceBridge moves voice over javax.sound.sampled + plain UDP datagrams, feeding the CI-proven G.711/RtpPacket/JitterBuffer stack (its device-free frame packing and little-endian conversion are asserted; the four worker threads that touch a mic, a speaker or a socket are verified live, per the standing rule). 99 new headless cases (88 wonderland-modules across eight softphone suites — the crown G711 encode/decode sweeps over every short — + 11 lg3d-apps); ShippedModuleSetTest now discovers eight providers; coverageFloors[wonderland-modules] raised [0.980, 0.935] → [0.985, 0.945] (measured 98.88 % / 95.32 %). No audio, process or network live call is claimed from CI.
  • Wonderland avatar animation lands on COLLADA keyframes (wonderland-modules + wonderland-renderer + wonderland-avatars + wonderland-desktop, M7c) — the third M7 replacement: the 2006 AvatarJME drove skeletal animation through jME-1.x's Animator against a .jme binary pool that was fetched by Java Web Start and is unrecoverable, so the port ships a COLLADA-driven keyframe animator instead, consuming the animation-name string the wire has carried since M6b (AvatarTriggerState.lastAnimationName). The parse half lives in wonderland-modules/collada: ColladaAnimation keeps the raw <library_animations> vocabulary — sources with their float data and accessor stride (under <technique_common>, as the 1.4.1 spec nests it), samplers with hash-stripped INPUT/OUTPUT refs, the interpolation attribute and the flat index pairs, channels with the target string untouched — and the Blender group-animation flatten merges child records into the parent; interpretation deliberately does not live here. The playable half is a new pure org.jdesktop.wonderland.renderer.animation package: ChannelTarget (the node/sid.element[.ARRAY] vocabulary), KeyframeTrack (right- continuous LINEAR/STEP sampling, clamped outside the key span), AnimationClip (per-node tracks composed into a Matrix4d pose via Rodrigues), ColladaClips (the raw-to-playable factory: the stride-4 axis+angle rotation bundle, the stride-3 Euler refusal — dropped, not misread — BEZIER collapses to LINEAR, times normalise to t=0, an unresolvable channel degrades instead of throwing), SyntheticClips (the idle/walking/waving fallback so an unrigged body never freezes, exactly as on the 2006 desktop), AnimationLibrary and AvatarAnimationDirector (the playback policy on an injected clock: LOOPING names wrap, gestures play once then revert to idle, the alias table maps walk/run to walking, unknown names fall back to idle). The live half is probe-only: AvatarRenderer now builds one nested LOCAL TransformGroup per Collada node (replacing M6b's flat world-matrix soup, so an animated joint drags its subtree), ticks the director from a 33 ms daemon clock wired to WonderlandWorldContainer mount/unmount, and writes the sampled pose overrides each tick; a trigger press feeds the director immediately. The bundled humanoid-a.dae gained hand-authored walking (bob + axis-angle sway) and idle clips against its real node id — bodies B and C deliberately ship no rig, exercising the synthetic path. 77 new headless cases (7 ColladaAnimationTest, 70 across eight renderer suites, the crown AvatarAnimationBundledPoolTest driving the REAL shipped .dae bytes through the whole chain with no stubbing); wonderland-renderer floor raised [0.530, 0.560] → [0.660, 0.660] (measured 66.9 % / 67.0 %). Live playback is verified on the desktop probe, per the standing rule.
  • The Wonderland pdfviewer lands on Apache PDFBox (wonderland-modules + lg3d-apps, M7b) — the second M7 replacement: the 2006 pdfviewer rasterised pages with jpedalSTD, a dead library with no maintained JDK 21 build, and the modern equivalent — Apache PDFBox — is already in-tree behind this desktop's own PDF Viewer, so the port now ships ONE PDF backend, not two. The module keeps the M4 headless shape: PdfViewModel is the pure document model — the EMPTY/LOADING/LOADED/ERROR lifecycle (a blank source is refused so a typo cannot blank an open document; a late markLoaded for a replaced document is refused; a zero-page document is an ERROR, not a loaded one), the clamped 1-based paging walk (gotoPage clamps into range, nextPage / previousPage stick at the edges), and the clamped zoom ([0.1, 8.0], a NaN or non-positive scale resets to 100 %, and zoomOut clamps at the minimum itself so a step from 0.25 cannot fall through the nonsense-reset path); the pixels live behind a new PageRasterizer seam that speaks only encoded PNG bytes and an int page count — no AWT type crosses into the module — reached through the PdfViewerPlugin installRasterizerFactory slot (the M6b/M7a installer idiom), with a shipped NoopPageRasterizer so a headless JVM lands an open honestly on ERROR instead of pretending. The live half is the lg3d-apps PdfBoxRasterizer, a thin adapter over the existing pdfviewer/PdfDocument: it keeps exactly one parsed document open (page flips must not re-load), replaces it on a URI change, PNG-encodes through ImageIO for the seam, and returns −1 / null on missing or unparsable files. Because PDFBox runs under java.awt.headless=true (the standing PdfDocumentTest precedent), this adapter is CI-provable, not probe-only: PdfBoxRasterizerTest resolves and rasterises real generated A4 PDFs and asserts the PNG decodes back at the expected ~595×842 px for 100 % and ~half for 50 % zoom. 30 new headless cases (14 PdfViewModelTest, 9 PdfViewerPluginTest incl. the ServiceLoader discovery, 7 PdfBoxRasterizerTest); the module joins the shipped set (now seven). Live in-world page display is still verified on the desktop, per the standing rule.
  • The Wonderland videoplayer lands on OpenJFX Media (wonderland-modules + lg3d-apps, M7a) — the first of the four M7 replacements, and the answer to the retired javax.media (JMF): the 2006 videoplayer drove JMF's Player / MediaHandler, which has no JDK 21 build and is unrecoverable, so the modern equivalent is OpenJFX Media / MediaPlayer / MediaView — the same engine already in-tree behind the Web Browser. The module is split the pure-vs-sink way every Wonderland slice now is. The pure half lives in a new org.jdesktop.wonderland.modules.videoplayer package with no toolkit type at all (so wonderland-modules' hard headless floor holds): MediaSurface is the sink seam (open / play / pause / stop / seekTo / setVolume / release), VideoTransport is the guarded lifecycle machine — load refuses a null/empty URI and stops the old media first, play rewinds from ENDED/STOPPED, pause only lands from PLAYING, seek clamps to [0, duration] but stays unclamped for a live/unknown-length stream, tick advances only while PLAYING and walks once to ENDED + a single stop, and setVolume clamps with NaN → silent — Playlist is the wrapping-cursor catalog whose removeAt keeps the cursor on the successor, and VideoPlayerPlugin is the ServiceLoader provider holding a static installSurfaceFactory slot (the M6b installer idiom): headless it drives a shipped NoopMediaSurface, and tickAndAdvance moves the cursor before the load so an ended item is never replayed and its successor never skipped. The live sink is lg3d-apps' JfxMediaSurface — it boots the toolkit via the browser's JFXPanel-on-the-EDT pattern, marshals every mutating call through Platform.runLater, and converts a bare file path to a file: URI for local playlist items; it wires in through VideoPlayerPlugin.installSurfaceFactory, so lg3d-apps gains an implementation project(':wonderland-modules') dep (no cycle: wonderland-modules depends only on wonderland-common). JavaFX is initialised only in this 2D-desktop JVM, never in the Java 3D process, exactly the standing constraint. 56 new headless cases (VideoTransportTest, PlaylistTest, VideoPlayerPluginTest incl. the ServiceLoader discovery and the auto-advance ordering), so coverageFloors[wonderland-modules] branch rises 0.930 → 0.935 (measured 98.52 % / 93.71 %). JfxMediaSurface is compile-checked in CI; live playback is verified on the desktop, not claimed as tested headless.
  • The Wonderland scene-graph bridge lands — a cell's world mounts inside the lg3d desktop (wonderland-desktop, new module) — M6c1, the first slice of the desktop integration milestone, and the first Wonderland module to depend on lg3d-core (strictly one-way: nothing in lg3d-core imports Wonderland). A loaded cell finally has somewhere to *live*: M6a/M6b build a renderer's BranchGroup, and this slice is what mounts it into the desktop's virtual universe and keeps it there as the server moves it. The slice is split the same pure-vs-probe way as wonderland-renderer.
