The pure half is CellFrameBridge, the mount/unmount/transform/visibility *decision* layer: it owns the mounted-set (a LinkedHashSet, so the snapshot is in mount order), guards a null cellId or renderer, ignores a double mount and an unmount of a cell that is not mounted, drops a transform or visibility update for a cell that unmounted between the server message and the render tick, and folds the CellTransform through M6a's WorldTransformMath into the row-major double[16] — but it never touches a Jogamp type: the *how* goes through the FrameMounter seam interface, so every decision is headless-tested against a recording stub (including that the translation lands on the last column, indices 3/7/11, and that a null transform degrades to the identity feed rather than throwing). WonderlandWorldContainer implements that seam for real — it extends lg3d-core's Component3D and wraps each mounted renderer's scene in its own ALLOW_TRANSFORM_WRITE TransformGroup, so applyTransform is a live setTransform — and is probe-only: its constructor reaches through AppConnectorPrivate and cannot run headless; only its type-only scene-extraction branch (extractScene: ModelRenderer / AvatarRenderer → its BranchGroup, anything else → null) is package-private and asserted in CI. WonderlandDesktop is the bootstrap (installRenderer() filling M6b's installer slot once, then cellLoaded / cellUnloaded / cellTransformUpdate driving the bridge), and WonderlandDesktopPlugin registers the whole thing as an M4 WonderlandPlugin ServiceLoader provider — dispose() unmounts every cell, and the bridge it discovers is checked by a real ServiceLoader.load in the test. 27 new headless cases (19 CellFrameBridgeTest, 5 WonderlandDesktopPluginTest, 3 WonderlandWorldContainerTest), so coverageFloors[wonderland-desktop] starts at [line: 0.420, branch: 0.540] (measured 43.8 % / 61.5 % — the gap is exactly the probe-only Component3D / bootstrap classes, the same honest shape as wonderland-renderer's floor). What M6c1 deliberately does not claim: the container's setVisible is a documented no-op until the Switch node is wired per cell, and the SwingNode HUD / login panels, the .lgcfg start-menu descriptor and the pick / input routing are M6c2. Live mounting is verified by launching the desktop + a bundled world through the in-JVM probe (lg3d-core/AGENTS.md) and reading the lgscreen-0-N.png screencapture — not claimed as tested in CI, per the standing rule.

It is a new module and not inside wonderland-client by design: wonderland-client runs its 164-case suite under java.awt.headless=true at a hard [0.980, 0.950] floor, and the repo rule is that Jogamp scene-graph objects (Shape3D, GeometryArray, BranchGroup, Appearance, Texture) cannot be constructed there — dropping the renderer into wonderland-client would add uncoverable Java 3D lines and break that floor. M6b (avatar renderer, replacing AvatarCell's deferred null) and M6c (2D+3D desktop integration hosting a cell's BranchGroup in lg3d-core's Frame3D / SceneGraphView) re-plan as each unblocks, per the migration's every-slice-requires-reconfirmation rule.

Three packages: M5a collada is a namespace-safe, DOCTYPE/entity-refusing DOM reader of COLLADA 1.4.1 — the asset header, geometries (source stride/count and the packed-index positions() walk), nodes with every transform folded to an org.jogamp.vecmath.Matrix4d (the column-major <matrix>, the degrees→radians <rotate>, the <lookat> basis and its degenerate identity, the component-defaulted translate/scale), the effect/material/image inventory and the texture-path chase, and tolerant numeric coercion (a bad token contributes nothing, never an abort). M2 was re-sliced by what CI can actually verify headless (the excluded AWT peer means a live scene graph is not testable, and the repo mandates per-module coverage), so M2b ships the first code that does real work yet still depends on nothing beyond wonderland-common + the JDK, with no lg3d-core / Java 3D import: CellSelectionRegistry (the process-wide singleton that registers / reads back the M2a CellSelectionSPI, blanking the slot only when the *same* instance unregisters it, so a stale provider cannot drop the current one); the headless view / renderer contracts ClientView and CellRenderer (interfaces that name no scene-graph type — only the common CellID / CellTransform / CellStatus data they trade); and the comms response substrate the M3 session will sit on — the ConnectionFailure / LoginFailure / ServerUnavailable exception hierarchy (with the cause-message-folding LoginFailureException(Throwable) shape pinned), the LoginParameters / WonderlandServerInfo value types, and the WaitResponseListener / OKErrorResponseListener blocking request-reply pair (a caller parked in waitForResponse wakes when the reader thread feeds responseReceived, and the OK/Error/unexpected three-way dispatch routes it — exercised with a helper thread, no socket). 16 new headless cases (CellSelectionRegistryTest + ResponseListenerTest + CommsValueTypesTest, on M2a's 8) cover every line and all 16 branches, so coverageFloors[wonderland-client] rises to [line: 0.950, branch: 0.900] (measured 100 % / 100 %) — the branch floor is real now that the module has branch logic, replacing M2a's 0.000 placeholder. What is deliberately not here is everything that reaches Cell itself: the Cell base class, the connection / session layer (BaseConnection / WonderlandSession), the login package and the client/jme renderer all pull lg3d-core (Java 3D) and the jME scene-graph shim, so they land as M2c, probe-verified in-JVM per lg3d-core/AGENTS.md rather than claimed green; they proceed only after this PR lands and the direction is re-confirmed.
  • The Wonderland client's cell layer starts landing bottom-up (wonderland-client, src/main/java/…/client/cell/, src/test/java/…/cell/) — M2a, the first increment of the migration plan's M2 milestone. The full M2 (port client/jme + cellrenderer onto Jogamp org.jogamp.java3d) cannot land as one PR, so M2a ships only the self-contained cell *leaf* slice that depends on nothing beyond wonderland-common + the JDK: the @CellFactory, @CellComponentFactory and @UsesCellComponent annotations, the CellFactorySPI / CellComponentFactorySPI / CellSelectionSPI SPIs, the AssetPreloader callback interface and CellCreationException. Two headless suites (8 cases: CellFactorySpiTest + CellRegistryAnnotationsTest) pin the shape the M2b registry and renderer compile against — above all the generic covariant-default-state contract <T extends CellServerState> T getDefaultCellServerState(Properties), whose anonymous implementations prove a caller assigns the erased return back to ModelCellServerState with no cast, exactly what the decompiled CellServerState subclasses rely on. wonderland-client graduates from M0's scaffold to a building, testing module: its build.gradle now declares the wonderland-common dependency and the JUnit 5 + AssertJ + JaCoCo wiring, and a new coverageFloors[wonderland-client] entry ([line: 0.900, branch: 0.000]) gates it — the slice is interfaces and annotations whose classfiles carry no executable lines, so the floor is measured against CellCreationException, the only coded class, at 100 %; it rises with M2b's real logic. No lg3d-core / Java 3D import — the module's first real logic arrived in M2b (the cell selection registry and the comms response substrate, both still headless); everything that reaches Cell itself — the base class, the connection / session layer and the client/jme renderer — lands as M2c, probe-verified in-JVM per lg3d-core/AGENTS.md, and proceeds only after this PR lands and the direction is re-confirmed.
  • The Wonderland wire protocol is now a tested contract (wonderland-common, src/test/java/…/messages/, …/comms/messages/, …/cell/messages/) — M1, the second milestone on the migration plan. M0 shipped the ~150-class data model compiling green on JDK 21 but with no proof that its Java-serialisation shape still worked; that shape *is* the wire contract between the ported client and the M3 Spring Boot session server (M3 carries these exact bytes over a BinaryWebSocketHandler), so any decompilation drift in a field name, an erased generic, a serialVersionUID or the Externalizable MessageID envelope would silently corrupt the protocol at runtime. Three new suites add 43 round-trip cases on top of M0's 77, every one of them packing a message through MessagePacker.pack(msg, clientID) and reading it back through MessagePacker.unpack(buf) — the same two entry points M3 will call: MessagePackerTest (11) pins the MessageID Externalizable path (long value + Long.MIN_VALUE "no-reply-to" sentinel + the generateMessageID() monotonic counter), the ErrorMessage cause/text pair, ProtocolSelectionMessage with a concrete DefaultProtocolVersion, the MessageList nested-message case, the empty WonderlandSetupMessage, the clientID short including 0 and negatives, and that two consecutive packs in the same JVM stay independent — the pin for WonderlandObjectOutputStream.descToId being read-only; CommsMessagesCodecTest (7) pins the session handshake: the AttachClient / AttachedClient / DetachClient trio, the SessionInternalConnectionType marker subclass surviving as its own class (not the ConnectionType base), and SessionInitializationMessage carrying a BigInteger session id alongside a WonderlandIdentity; CellMessagesCodecTest (25) covers every concrete subclass under common/cell/messages/ — the CellEditMessage family (Create / Delete / Duplicate / Reparent each with its EditType), the CellServerState{Request,Response,Set,Update}Message group with AvatarCellServerState / ModelCellServerState concrete subclasses resolving back to their own class (that is what ScannedClassLoader.getInstance(Class) needs), the Component add / remove messages with the ComponentAction enum, the Client state messages, the CellHierarchy{,Unload}Message pair (which carries the jME BoundingVolume + CellTransform + CellClientState triple that M2's renderer will consume), MovableAvatarMessage (the only coreClass message that crosses every one of the nine cached class descriptors — Vector3f, Quaternion, CellID, CellMessage, Message, etc. — in a single pack), the MovableMessage MOVED / MOVE_REQUEST action split, and MovableMessageResponse / ViewCreateResponseMessage. The raw-Set field on CellServerStateUpdateMessage — an artefact of Fernflower erasing the generic — is exercised with a ComponentHolder wrapper so the hashCode-based collection still resolves after deserialisation. Two shim bugs surfaced on the way and were fixed: the Set cast had to be a two-step through Set<?> to keep -Xlint quiet, and CellHierarchyMessage does not carry the cell name on the AVATAR_CELL_{ADDED,REMOVED} branches, which the test asserts rather than papers over. Measured coverage jumped from 17.56% / 17.90% to 32.36% / 21.48%, so coverageFloors[wonderland-common] is raised to [line: 0.300, branch: 0.200] in the same PR. The migration doc M1 row is flipped to 🟨 in progress and its session/host server decision is now recorded as Spring Boot 3 (embedded Tomcat + Spring WebSocket + REST controllers) rather than the earlier "plain java.net / java.nio" placeholder — chosen because the client already needs an HTTP surface for WFS, and one Spring Boot process gives both transports from the same lifecycle. M2 (Jogamp scene-graph renderer), M3 (the Spring Boot session server itself), M4 (NetBeans-layer plugin loader), M5 (asset pipeline + bundled worlds), M6 (2D + 3D desktop integration) and M7 (voicebridge / avatar / animation / videoplayer / pdfviewer) still proceed only after this PR lands and the direction is re-confirmed.
  • The Wonderland migration begins with a JDK-21 data-model foundation (wonderland-common, wonderland-client, wonderland-server, wonderland-modules; docs/wonderland-migration.md) — the repo has shipped wonderland/Wonderland.jar (the 400 MB Java-5 installer, .gitignored) for years with no way to build or run it on a current toolchain. M0 is the first PR on the approved milestone plan (docs/wonderland-migration.md records the subsystem inventory, the per-milestone parity table, and every rebuild-vs-port decision for the unrecoverable tech). What landed: four Gradle modules wired into settings.gradle and inheriting the root subprojects block (JDK 21 toolchain, JaCoCo, Checkstyle, CycloneDX); 146 classes decompiled with Fernflower from wonderland-common.jar + wonderland-wfs.jar and hand-migrated to JDK 21 (vecmath imports renamed to org.jogamp.vecmath, 11 raw-collection for-each loops recovered, 4 JAXB XmlAdapter subclasses re-parameterised, ChecksumList parameterised + given its erased @XmlElement(type = Checksum.class) so JAXB actually marshals on JDK 21); ScannedClassLoader rebuilt from sun.misc.Service + scannotation onto java.util.ServiceLoader + org.reflections:reflections: 0.10.2 while preserving its raw-Iterator public surface so CellServerStateFactory stays source-compatible; a from-scratch 10-file in-tree com.jme.* shim (math.{Vector3f,Quaternion,Matrix3f,Matrix4f, FastMath}, bounding.{BoundingVolume,BoundingBox,BoundingSphere}, renderer.ColorRGBA, scene.state.MaterialState) that implements exactly the surface the ported data model calls, because jME 1.x was fetched via Java Web Start at launch and is *not* in Wonderland.jar — no bytecode to port; javax.xml.bind restored against jakarta.xml.bind:jakarta.xml.bind-api: 2.3.3 + org.glassfish.jaxb:jaxb-runtime:2.3.9 (the 2.3.x line still uses the javax.xml.bind package name). 77 headless JUnit-5 tests across com.jme.{math,bounding}, Math3DUtils, CellTransform (both the pure-shim transform/sub/clone path and the vecmath mul/invert path), ChecksumList (an end-to-end JAXB round-trip that also proves the dependency wiring), and ScannedClassLoader (stable singleton, drainable iterators, ClassScanningError cause wrapping). Measured 17.56% line / 17.90% branch on the new module, floor set to coverageFloors[line: 0.150, branch: 0.150] and raised per milestone. .gitignore gained an anchored /wonderland/ rule so the 400 MB installer stays out without also hiding the wonderland-common/src/main/java/org/jdesktop/wonderland/ package tree. No milestone claims global 100% parity; M1 (client/cell + client/comms protocol round-trips), M2 (Jogamp scene-graph renderer), M3 (rebuilt session server to replace GlassFish/SGS/MINA), M4 (NetBeans-layer plugin loader), M5 (asset pipeline + bundled worlds), M6 (2D + 3D desktop integration via SwingNode) and M7 (voicebridge / avatar / animation / videoplayer / pdfviewer) proceed only after this PR lands and the direction is re-confirmed. darkstar + sas/sasxremwin/xremwin are dropped outright: their scene/applet functions are already covered by the Jogamp stack plus SwingNode (see docs/swingnode.md).
  • A published page demonstrating the language in everyday use (lg3d-mandela/docs/USAGE.md, mirrored on the GitHub Pages site as documentation/mandela/docs/USAGE.md) — the module had a reference, an architecture and a history, and nothing that answered *what do I write this in for, on a Tuesday*. The new page is a demonstration rather than a manual, and every block of it was executed rather than recalled: one ~80-line program that does what almost every desktop script does (walk a tree with fs.list + fs.isDirectory, scan the text it found with indexOf/substring in a loop, classify with a match expression, answer through json.stringify) followed by the CLI's real output, which shows 10 shipped programs, the 8 wired gate tasks, and the security model in a single JSON field — the script could read the tree but env.get came back refused by the host (PermissionError). A table then puts the four hosts side by side with what each actually grants, read out of the code that builds the engine: the CLI's desktop(root) at 50 M steps, Espresso's mandela-run/-check/-bytecode/template actions on the console() profile (no files at all — an unsaved buffer is not a sandbox), the browser's webPage() at 5 M steps with page/inject/note bound and println *bound* to the browser log rather than granted, and any JVM through the facade or JSR-223. The page also documents what the host accepts instead of a regular expression — the // @match glob is *, ? and literals, translated by the host — closes with the four rules a first script learns (-s DIR, an immutable let, + refusing Str + number, and Str.indexOf taking one argument), and reproduces real check, dump and runaway-eval transcripts with the exit codes a build can branch on. The site copy is the module copy's mirror with the links that leave documentation/ made absolute, both module indexes and the site READMEs list it, and the portal gained a card in each language; the two stale "VM instruction set" blurbs in the site README were corrected on the way past, since no guide in the tree contains one.
  • A published history of the language (lg3d-mandela/docs/HISTORY.md, mirrored on the GitHub Pages site as documentation/mandela/docs/HISTORY.md) — the module told you what Mandela is and how it is built, and never once why it is called *Mandela*, who made it, or when any of it arrived. The new page answers all three: the homage to Nelson Mandela stated as the record has it (imprisoned from 1962 until his release on 11 February 1990, president 1994–1999, died 5 December 2013 — he did not die in prison, which is the telling this page exists to correct), the creator attribution to Jean-François Landreville publishing as Dr. Land Evil, the four reasons a language of its own was written rather than bought, and a dated milestone table read out of git log — the module landing whole in one commit on 2026-10-10, then the scripts, the guides, the BDD suite, the defect campaign and the eight gates. The module's copy is canonical and the site copy is its mirror with the links that leave documentation/ made absolute, exactly as the other four guides are; both indexes link it and the portal gained a card in each language.
  • The Help Center now writes its own What's New page from the CHANGELOG (lg3d-apps, org.jdesktop.lg3d.apps.help + scripts/mandela/) — the built-in JavaHelp guide used to say only what a person remembered to write into a topic, so it went stale on the day its refresh PR merged, and the desktop's own release notes were unreadable from inside the desktop. whats-new.mnd now renders the [Unreleased] section and the three most recently released ones into a nineteenth topic (whats-new.html), which the existing generateHelpSearchIndex task indexes like any other because it globs every *.html in the directory, so release notes are full-text searchable from the Search tab. The same script is the gate: run without its write word it re-renders in memory and fails when the committed topic no longer matches CHANGELOG.md, which is what turns "remember to refresh the help" into a build failure, and it reports how many Added entries are still not named in any topic — the candidates for a real new page. The rendered topic is a committed generated file: edit CHANGELOG.md and re-run :lg3d-mandela:whatsNewRefresh, never the HTML.
  • Project Mandela's module documentation is now published on the GitHub Pages portal (documentation/, mirrors lg3d-mandela/docs/) — the four module guides (overview, architecture, development, functional analysis) live under documentation/mandela/docs/ and are reached from the bilingual landing page, where two new cards open them through viewer.html. The links that leave documentation/ were rewritten to absolute GitHub URLs so they resolve on the published site — Pages serves this directory as the site root, so a ../ link 404s there even though it works in the module tree — and the site README gained the matching structure entry and a bilingual *Project Mandela* section.
  • A crash-report pipeline that turns a crash into a GitHub issue without ever holding a credential (lg3d-core, org.jdesktop.lg3d.displayserver.crash) — the desktop has had a crash *dialog* since 2006 and no way to make one into a bug report: its button opened a bare tracker page and expected the reporter to retype what the dialog was already showing. Eight classes now do that end to end. CrashSignature hashes the root cause plus up to six non-synthetic frames to 12 hex characters — deliberately *not* the message and not the version, so an upgrade does not re-file a known bug and a crash loop stays one bug; its ofNarrative gives a hand-written report, which has no frames to sign, an identity taken from its own words and normalised for whitespace — reformatting a draft does not open a second archive entry, and two hand-written bugs are no longer merged into one by the builder's no-throwable fallback, which hashes the message and therefore gave every draft whose title went to the summary the same bucket; Redactor replaces home paths, the runtime user name, e-mail addresses, socket paths, GitHub / AWS / Google keys and key = secret pairs before anything is written, with linear patterns so a report cannot be a ReDoS against its own author; ReportEnvironment collects the twelve fields that diagnose without identifying anyone (version, JVM, OS, display, locale, memory — no user name, no host name); CrashReport is the one immutable text that is simultaneously the spool file, the clipboard content and the issue body, so what a reporter copies is what a maintainer reads; CrashStore keeps ~/.lg3d/crash-reports grouped by signature with an occurrence count, written atomically and pruned under both a 50-report and an 8 MB ceiling; IssuePrefill builds the github.com/landrevillejf/ProjectLookingGlass/issues/new link — titled, labelled crash, assigned, with the body clipped to a 7600-byte *encoded* budget rather than a character count, because percent-escaping triples what a URL can actually carry; CrashReporter is the facade on one daemon thread; and CrashWatcher is the Thread.setDefaultUncaughtExceptionHandler hook installed on the first line of Main.main, which still prints the dump the JDK would have printed — installing a handler *silences* it — and still chains to the handler the host already had. There is no HTTP call anywhere in it. The only network-facing artefact is a link handed to the browser, so the person stays the one who submits, the review step an unattended upload would skip is kept, and a kiosk image has no token to leak.
  • The noise rules are what makes it usable (lg3d-core, CrashReporter) — one signature opens one browser tab per session, a bug already in the archive is not reopened by a new session, and a per-session budget caps how many *distinct* bugs may interrupt anyone; past it reports are still captured, silently, because capture is local and cheap and interruption is the only real cost. A report a *person* asked for — the dialog's new Report this bug button, the manual Bug Reporter app to come — overrides every one of those rules. Everything is configurable without a rebuild through lg.crashreport.*: enabled, repo, labels, assignee, maxPerSession, dir, maxReports, maxBytes. The assignee is the "notify the admin" answer: GitHub mails the person pre-filled in the link, so there is no SMTP configuration and no address baked into a build. A kill switch never silences a hand-written report, and only the literal word false flips it — a typo is not a reason to go back to twenty years of unreported crashes.
  • A SEVERE log record is a bug report too (lg3d-core, LogHandler) — the trigger is no longer only an escaping exception, and the record's own text is now carried into the report: without that, the desktop's most common complaint (cannot open {0}, throwing nothing) filed a form with nothing in it. describe does the {i} substitution by hand, because MessageFormat eats apostrophes. The link the pipeline assembles is handed to the error dialog through setReportLink — off the EDT, on a volatile, since a slow disk must not delay the warning — and nothing at all is captured when there is neither a stack nor a text.
  • 123 headless tests for the crash package (lg3d-core, src/test/java/org/jdesktop/lg3d/displayserver/crash/) — one suite per class, none constructing a widget or touching the network, with a recording sink standing in for the browser. Writing them found six defects that reading the same code had missed: every *automatic* capture was bypassing dedupe and the budget (doReport passed explicit = true, so a crash loop would have opened a browser tab per exception), a console echo that threw skipped the chained host handler, a second install() stacked a second watcher and captured every crash twice, a re-read archive could no longer tell an uncaught exception from a log record (CrashStore.read hardcoded the reporter), a prune() that mutated the list it was iterating would have thrown ConcurrentModificationException from inside the crash reporter — a crash in the bug reporter — while its byte ceiling deleted the very report that had just been written, and a SEVERE record with no throwable filed a report with no content in it. Designing the Bug Reporter panel that consumes it turned up three more, all on the archive's round trip: a *named evidence file* kept the absolute path a file chooser hands back — the reporter's own account name, in a public issue, while addAttachment' javadoc claimed it had been shortened; record.json stored none of the human half of a report, so re-filing a stored bug came back as "[MINOR] severe error" with no steps, no expected/actual and no evidence — the work a person typed, discarded; and the body's (no message) placeholder was read back as an actual message, giving a re-filed report a title ending in ": (no message)". CrashStoreTest.manualNarrativeSurvivesTheArchive pins the round trip now.
  • A Bug Reporter app — the manual half of the crash-reporting tool (lg3d-apps, org.jdesktop.lg3d.apps.bugreporter; lg3d-core, Desktop2DAppRegistry) — the automatic capture structurally cannot see the bugs that never throw: a task bar that wraps, a splash that stays, a resize that loses a workspace. Start Menu → Utilities → Bug Reporter opens a form for exactly those: subject, repro steps, expected/actual, severity, a typed evidence list (paths are named, never uploaded, and reduced to bare redacted file names before anything is filed), a live preview of the *exact* issue text, and the same prefilled github.com/.../issues/new link the crash pipeline produces — still no token, still the human pressing the real button. A crash already in the spool can be attached, and the filed report then keeps the crash's signature, trace and environment with the human narrative layered on top, so one bug never splits into two issues; a hand-written report with no crash signs itself through CrashSignature.ofNarrative. One BugReporterPanel serves both desktops — TitledSwingWindow/SwingNode in 3D, an MDI internal frame via PANEL_APPS in 2D — with all the consequences in a headless BugReportDraft (a non-blank subject is the only blocker, everything else is advice), disk and browser work off the EDT on a named daemon executor, and no modal dialog anywhere. 17 headless tests (BugReportDraftTest 10, BugReporterPanelTest 7).
  • Internationalisation of the shell — the desktop can now speak French (lg3d-core, org.jdesktop.lg3d.i18n; lg3d-apps, Control Center) — the 2006 codebase shipped zero user-facing i18n machinery (the three ExceptionStrings.properties files are remnants of a bundle system that no longer exists), so every label was welded into the Java. Tranche 1 builds the mechanism and translates the *shell*: LgLocale resolves the run's language once at start (-Dlg.locale > the persisted desktop.locale preference > the JVM default, and any unknown pin lands on English — visible-but-English beats blank or crashed), and Messages.tr(key, args…) reads messages.properties (English source of code) or its French twin through a ResourceBundle.Control whose fallback is *null*, so an unsupported host locale never hijacks the language. A miss echoes the key and a broken MessageFormat pattern echoes the pattern — the painting path cannot throw. Extracted: the whole 2D shell (taskbar, start menu, tray, pager, run dialog, context menu, About box, launch notifications, power/exit confirms), the 3D chrome (start-menu panel/disc/orbit labels, dock folder stacks, the 3D run card), and the .lgcfg descriptors *without touching the 83 XML files* — both readers look up lgcfg.<slug-of-name>.name/.desc and fall back to the XML literal, so an untranslated descriptor simply keeps its published name and startmenu-audit.mnd is untouched. Control Center → Customization gains a Language selector (System default / English / Français, persisted, applied at the next desktop restart — no hot-swap by design, a live scene graph re-tinting its own text was never on the table). 288 keys in each bundle — 97 shell labels plus 191 start-menu descriptor entries — pinned three ways: LgLocaleTest/MessagesTest headless, a descriptor round trip in Desktop2DMenuConfigTest, and the new scripts/mandela/i18n-keys.mnd gate in :lg3d-mandela:repositoryChecks (every tr literal exists, en/fr key sets are equal, {n} placeholders agree). All Test tasks run with lg.locale=en so the extraction cannot quietly change what existing assertions read. The apps themselves (~2,000 strings) are tranche 2, one PR per start-menu group.
  • The runaway-loop guard finally has a test, and two gates join the repository checks (lg3d-mandela, vm/VM + MachineHostTest; scripts/mandela/) — the step budget is the sandbox's headline promise (a mistyped loop { } cannot hang the desktop) yet it was the one machine limit asserted *nowhere*: MachineHostTest pinned the call-depth and host re-entrancy guards, but a change to the retired-loop check could regress silently. Three tests now pin it — a loop/while runaway is retired at the ceiling and the message quotes maxSteps back (the number a host tunes against), honest work *under* the ceiling runs (the other side of the >), and tripping it is recoverable, so a host can try around untrusted code and keep its engine. Two gates join :lg3d-mandela:repositoryChecks (seven at this writing, eight with the What's New gate above): legacy-j3d.mnd turns the Java 3D migration rule into a build truth — no source the build compiles may import a pre-migration package (javax.media.j3d / javax.vecmath / com.sun.j3d), scoped so the do-not-edit lg3d-docs, the retired lg3d-awt toolkit and the two deserialisation shims stay legitimately out of scope — and scripts-hygiene.mnd closes the rot neither the compiler nor Gradle's own wiring can see: a gate pointing at a missing script, a registered task the repositoryChecks aggregate silently omits, or a shipped .mnd absent from the scripts README (and vice versa). Both were proven to bite on a planted defect before shipping green.
  • Two Mandela scripts now police the desktop's own runtime configuration (scripts/mandela, lg3d-mandela/build.gradle, root AGENTS.md) — the automation had checked documents and versions, but two kinds of hand-written configuration that fail only at run time went unguarded, so the language was pointed at them. accelerators.mnd joins the gates: it reads the 2D desktop's global shortcut table straight from its source of truth (ShortcutMap.defaultBindings, expanding the alt shift 1..9 workspace loop against the real WorkspaceModel.MAX_COUNT) and scans every production source for a keystroke-spec literal, then fails on the three chords that are written correctly yet can never fire — a window-manager grab (a Super/Meta chord, or Ctrl+Alt+arrow, which Mutter/Xwayland eats before the JVM sees it), a binding that shadows the window switcher's Alt+` which ShortcutMap must leave unbound, and two shell bindings that normalise to one stroke; an application chord that merely overlaps a live shell chord, or that two apps both bind, is printed for a human to weigh but never red-lines the build. It ships green and names 11 such overlaps to review. startmenu-categories.mnd is its report sibling (always exit 0, like todo-scan.mnd): it reads each live .lgcfg descriptor's name and description, scores them against a keyword vocabulary for the eight groups the menu uses, and flags the items whose declared menuGroup is beaten by a different group's own evidence — today Image Studio and Paint read as Media while filed under Utilities — a suggestion a maintainer weighs, never a failure, because category is a judgement. acceleratorsCheck is wired into :lg3d-mandela:repositoryChecks (now eleven gates) and startmenuCategories stands alone as a reporting task; scripts-hygiene.mnd proves both are documented and the gate is in the aggregate.

Fixed

  • The Background Manager offered the same panorama twice, and shipped a background directory nothing reads (lg3d-incubator) — found by scripts/mandela/bgconfigs.mnd as it was written. BgConfigFileReader appends every <BGURL> it reads without de-duplicating, and res/BgConfig.xml listed resources/Backgrounds/PyramidLakeSunrise/LgBgConf.lgbg twice, so the picker showed one panorama as two menu entries — the duplicate line is gone. The second defect was invisible from the config: the directory Backgrounds/DreamLakeReflrctions/ (the name misspelled) held a single JPEG and no LgBgConf.lgbg, so nothing could ever list it, while runtimeResources relocated its art into the shipped classpath tree regardless. That JPEG was byte-identical to lg3d-core/src/resources/images/background/DreamLakeReflections.jpg, which is the copy the desktop wallpaper cycle, the glassy taskbar and the Control Center's Appearance/Schedule panels actually resolve — so the relocated file was dead weight in every bundle, read by no code and no menu. The directory is deleted; the wallpaper itself is untouched, and the gate now fails if a background directory appears in the tree with no descriptor to offer it.
  • The released desktop could not open a Terminal: releaseBundle shipped neither the lg3d-terminal jar nor JNA (lg3d-core) — PR #428 put lg3d-terminal and net.java.dev.jna:jna / jna-platform on the hand-assembled :lg3d-core:run classpath, which is why the Terminal opened under ./gradlew :lg3d-core:run. The release bundle's lib/ never got them, so the shipped -cp "${HERE}/lib/*" offered a start-menu entry whose classes — and whose PTY library, since com.sun.jna.Native behind forkpty is what allocates the shell — were not on the classpath: NoClassDefFoundError on the first shell, on the user's machine, and invisible to CI because nothing compared the two lists. Both copies now carry all three, the bundle's own comment inventory names JNA beside JSch, and scripts/mandela/run-classpath.mnd is the gate that keeps them equal.
  • A Gradle/Maven project carrying its own distribution no longer reports "not available" (lg3d-apps) — BuildTools.launcher resolved a build tool by checking for a file literally named gradlew/mvnw at the project root and then falling back to gradle/ mvn on the system PATH. A project whose Gradle or Maven was unpacked at its root (or under .espresso/tools/) but had no wrapper script therefore resolved to nothing whenever the system tool was absent, and Espresso reported "Gradle is not available" for a project that shipped its own. Resolution now goes through ProjectToolchain: the wrapper first, then a project-carried distribution (.espresso/tools/gradle-*/apache-maven-*, then a root-level gradle-*/apache-maven-*), and the PATH fallback is removed entirely — a project builds with the exact tool Espresso provisioned into it, and the missing-tool message reads "not provisioned — no project Gradle/Maven" rather than pointing at a system install. BuildToolsTest pins the wrapper → project-distribution → empty priority and the absence of any PATH lookup, and GradleBuildToolsTest/MavenBuildToolsTest assert a provisioned project runs .espresso/tools/…/bin/gradle (or mvn) with JAVA_HOME set to the selected JDK.
  • A Gradle too old for the host JDK is now named as the cause, and the build pins that JDK past a wrapper that ignores JAVA_HOME (lg3d-apps) — Espresso's Build actions pinned the project's selected JDK as JAVA_HOME, and a real project still failed with *“Could not open cp_proj generic class cache for build file ‘…/build.gradle’”* over *“BUG! exception in phase ‘semantic analysis’ in source unit ‘_BuildScript_’ Unsupported class file major version 69”*. Reproduced from the log up: the same wrapper and the same Gradle 8.5, changing only the JDK — Java 25 fails in 4s, Java 21 succeeds in 6s — and deleting ~/.gradle/caches between two runs reproduces the failure byte-identically, so no cache was ever the problem. The message is Gradle’s wrapper around its embedded Groovy refusing a class file it predates (major 69 = Java 25; Gradle 8.5 reads up to 65 = Java 21), and the Java release is major − 44. JAVA_HOME had been discarded by the launcher Espresso chose: the project’s gradlew was a scaffolder’s few-line exec java -jar gradle-wrapper.jar "$@", which resolves java from PATH and so built on the host default. Three changes. BuildTools.gradleCommand now passes -Dorg.gradle.java.home=<jdk> beside the environment pin — a property the Gradle client reads from argv whatever the script does (verified against that very stub with no JAVA_HOME and system Java 25: the build then succeeds). ProjectToolchain credits a wrapper only when its text reads JAVA_HOME, so a stub yields to a distribution Espresso provisioned and stays the last resort rather than the first choice. And BuildTools.toolchainAdvice turns a major version in the log into *“this Gradle cannot read Java 25 classes — pick a JDK it supports for the project, or upgrade its wrapper; the cache message is a symptom, not the cause”*, which the status line prefers over the misleading headline — while a failure that names a cache and no version is a genuinely stale or half-deleted one, and gets that answer instead, with the daemon that still holds the deleted workspace open named beside it. 6 new headless cases: BuildToolsTest pins the argv property and feeds toolchainAdvice the verbatim log recorded from Gradle 8.5 on Java 25 (and the boundary cases NN − 44 must not invent); ProjectToolchainTest proves a JAVA_HOME-honouring wrapper still wins, a stub yields to a provisioned distribution, and a stub alone is still resolved; GradleBuildToolsTest asserts the advice, not the cache sentence, reaches the status line, and that the JDK travels into the argv of every action.
  • A Spring Boot port conflict now names the port, the process using it, and how to free it (lg3d-apps) — bootRun failed with *"Port 8080 was already in use"* and the status line echoed the failure headline, which told the user nothing they could act on. BuildTools.portInUseAdvice now detects the Spring Boot port-conflict pattern, extracts the port number, and runs lsof -ti :<port> (with a fallback to ss -tlnp) to find the PID, then ps -p <pid> -o comm= to name the process. The status line reads *"Port 8080 is in use by java (PID 12345); stop it or use --server.port=8081"* — the next port is the natural escape for a one-off conflict. When the tools are unavailable or the port is free by the time the check runs, the fallback names the port and the escape without a PID. The advice is wired into statusLine after toolchainAdvice, so a JDK mismatch still wins over a port conflict, and a port conflict wins over the generic failure headline. A new Free Port toolbar action (gradle-free-port) kills whatever process holds port 8080 (Spring Boot's default) by sending SIGTERM first (graceful shutdown) and escalating to SIGKILL when the process ignores it, then reports the result on the status line — *"Freed port 8080: java (PID 12345) stopped"* — so the user can re-run bootRun without manually hunting for the PID. 2 new headless cases: BuildToolsTest feeds the verbatim Spring Boot failure log and asserts the advice names the port and suggests the next port; GradleBuildToolsTest pins the eighth toolbar contribution.
  • The Web Server Console no longer vanishes from both start menus (lg3d-apps) — webserver.lgcfg carried a -- inside its XML comment ("the desktop classpath -- lg3d-apps does not depend on"), and -- is illegal within an XML comment, so the descriptor was not well-formed. Both discovery paths parse descriptors with a conformant parser and silently skip one that throws — the 3D desktop's DefaultConfigControl (via XMLDecoder) and the 2D desktop's Desktop2DMenuConfig (via DocumentBuilder, which logged SAXParseException ... The string "--" is not permitted within comments) — so the app was packaged correctly yet appeared in neither menu. The startmenu-audit.mnd gate could not catch it because it greps the descriptor text rather than parsing it. The comment prose is reworded to a colon, and a new LgcfgWellFormedTest parses every shipped .lgcfg so a malformed descriptor now fails the build instead of silently disappearing.
  • Neither *What's New* surface advertises unreleased work any more — both show released versions only (lg3d-apps, scripts/mandela, update-manager) — [Unreleased] is by definition work that has not shipped, so a person who opened a *What's New* inside a released build read a page advertising features their desktop does not have — the whole 1.69.0-dev section rendered above the versions they could actually run. Two surfaces carried the bug. The Help Center's topic is generated from CHANGELOG.md by scripts/mandela/whats-new.mnd, and its sectionsOf kept [Unreleased] first, then the three newest releases; it now renders the three newest released versions and never [Unreleased], matching the release archive beside it (releasesOf already skipped [Unreleased], so the two skins of one document had come to disagree). The Update Manager's "What's new in Project Looking Glass" dialog renders the same CHANGELOG.md through ChangelogManager.toHtml(), which appended every entry including [Unreleased]; it now skips that section, so the dialog names shipped work only — while getAllEntries() keeps the complete data and getEntry still never resolves a release number to [Unreleased]. The topic's own note, the archive index.html note, the script header, AGENTS.md and the scripts README.md each said "the [Unreleased] section plus the three newest releases"; every one now says released-only. whatsNewCheck still gates the committed pages byte for byte, HelpContentTest.whatsNewTopicIsGenerated still holds (the topic renders three <h2> version headings), and ChangelogManagerTest.testUnreleasedSectionIsNeitherRenderedNorResolved pins the dialog. The unreleased work is not lost: it stays in CHANGELOG.md and on GitHub, which is where a reader goes to see what is coming.
  • The sound mixer's covered air depended on the runner's sound card — P4.1 follow-up (wonderland-client) — JavaSoundBackend's clip-present path (open, start, loop, the per-control pose, stop, close, the re-load that replaces) ran only when AudioSystem.getClip() succeeded: 98.4 % on a dev box with speakers, 97.3 % on a headless CI with no mixer, which let the module's 0.980 floor — calibrated against the first — go red on the second. The gap is closed with tests, not by lowering the floor: a package-private ClipSource seam now feeds the backend its clips from anywhere — production passes exactly AudioSystem::getClip, unchanged — and 7 new JavaSoundBackendMixerTest cases drive the whole verb contract through a recording fake Clip, on CI and on a desktop identically, while the "device refused the line" catch is reproduced deterministically instead of left to the runner's luck. The class measures 100 % lines and branches. What no fake can prove keeps its clause in the class header: a real Clip must still move real air before "the pond splashes" is claimed.
  • The meeting complex's pond vanished between the .mtg and the renderer — roadmap P2.3 (wonderland-modules + wonderland-renderer) — a water record names no .dae, so the world fold skipped it and nothing else ever looked: JMEWaterInstance carried fifteen tokens that no reader read. Re-honoured in both halves the port can prove headless. WaterInstance parses the record — place, spin, scale, width/length, ground name — and never throws: a malformed line costs one pond, the fold's own rule; MtgSceneReader.readWaterInstances scans them beside the fold and ModelLoadResult.waterInstances carries them to the renderer (an empty list, never null, for every non-MTG artifact). WaterArt supplies the honest fixed-pipeline stand-in for jME's water shader: a seamless procedural tile — integer wave periods across, a dividing band family down, wrapped copies at both edges, so the seam tests are assertions a scrolling texture cannot pass by luck — plus per-axis scroll-offset maths that wrap every tile and hold a broken clock still rather than NaN, and planeOf folding a record into the five numbers its quad is built from. Placing the pond and driving TexCoordGeneration from a frame clock are Java 3D/probe work and are NOT asserted painted here, the same rule P2.2 set. 7 new WaterArtTest cases and the water parsing in MtgSceneReaderTest (suite of 23) green.
  • Walking into the clinic crashed on every resident, because a seeded AvatarCell was put on the wire as a plain CellClientState (wonderland-server + wonderland-client) — the same live walk-in this branch adds, one layer past the environment root. The clinic seeds named residents (Receptionist, Waiting Patient…), and WorldSeeder.seedCell maps an AvatarCellServerState to the client's AvatarCell — which *is* a ViewCell, whose setClientState reads a ViewCellClientState identity. But a resident is not a model cell, so it fell through to the non-model branch and got a plain CellClientState. A walking-in client loading cell after cell hit ClassCastException: CellClientState cannot be cast to ViewCellClientState in loadCell, each one logged SEVERE and fed to the crash reporter — a dialog per resident. The seeder now gives an avatar cell the ViewCellClientState its client class demands (an empty one — a resident has no session identity), so the wire matches the cell's contract the way the router already does for live view cells. ViewCell.setClientState additionally guards the cast: a foreign or legacy frame carrying some other state now leaves the identity unset instead of aborting the whole load, because a name label is not worth a second failure on top of the user's. WorldSeederTest pins the seeded state type, and MovableAvatarComponentTest.plainClientStateDoesNotBreakTheViewCellCast loads an AvatarCell from a plain CellClientState and asserts it does not throw.
  • A live walk-in crashed the desktop on entering any world, because the server broadcast an abstract class as the environment root (wonderland-client + wonderland-server) — the same walk-in this branch adds. WorldModel is a Spring @Service built by its no-arg constructor, which seeds the root cell with ENVIRONMENT_CLASS = org.jdesktop.wonderland.client.cell.EnvironmentCell, and that class was abstract. CellCacheBasicImpl.instantiateCell reflects the name the server pushes open with Constructor.newInstance, so on the transport thread every session's first cell load threw InstantiationException, logged it SEVERE, and LogHandler fed that to the crash reporter — the desktop's "severe error" dialog on the way in the door. It survived the suite because every environment test loaded a concrete fixture subclass (CacheableEnvCell, CacheableEnv) and none named the production default, while the router already names the *concrete* ViewCell directly — the asymmetry was the whole bug. EnvironmentCell adds nothing over Cell, so it is now concrete: instantiateCell succeeds on the default world, the cache's (EnvironmentCell) type-recognition cast is unchanged, and the fixture subclasses still extend it. CellCacheBasicImplTest .theDefaultEnvironmentClassIsInstantiableByTheCache loads EnvironmentCell.class.getName() — the exact string the server broadcasts — and asserts a non-null ACTIVE cell, so a future re-abstracting fails here rather than in a user's crash dialog.
  • A cell's width and depth were the square of the room, so the world browser's floor plan drew a 5.4 m exam room as a 58 m one (wonderland-server) — the position component's <bounds> are stored half-extents (putFootprint doubles them and multiplies by the cell's stretch, exactly as the .dep format stores a box), and the clinic's cells authored them as if they were the placed metres: hall-wlc.xml carried bounds = scale = 22 × 16, which the read turned into a 968 m lobby, and the floor reported 1152 × 2312 m. Only one surface showed it, which is why it survived so long: the 3D view never looks at cell bounds — WorldScene.extentOf sizes every model from the .dep's own modelBounds, falling back to the raw COLLADA positions — so the rooms rendered at their right size while the 2D plan preview, which reads Entry.footprint, drew them as overlapping blobs. Two readers of one world disagreeing is the defect; the number is only how it shows. All thirteen model cells now carry their model's true half-extent (0.506 for clinic-room, 0.5 for the desk, ground, sign and sofa, read off each .dep), and <scale> is left alone, because the scale *is* the metres. WorldCatalogTest and WorldRestControllerTest no longer pin a magic size: both assert the product — 2 × half-extent × stretch — with the half-extent named as what it is, so a future cell that authors metres fails a test instead of quietly redrawing the map.
  • Every cell heading in every world was silently dropped, so a turned object drew facing north and a poster read as missing art (wonderland-renderer) — WorldScene built both of its yaw matrices as new AxisAngle4f(yaw, 0, 1, 0), but vecmath's four-argument constructor is (x, y, z, angle): the heading landed in the axis slot and the angle became zero. Nothing threw, nothing failed to load, and the cell was still seated exactly where its world put it, which is what makes this the quietest defect in the port — the placement is right, only the direction is gone. Read back out of the clinic's own scene graph, all six wall cards and the three residents whose headings the world wrote came back m00 = 1, m02 = 0: a print authored a quarter-turn to hang flat against the east wall drew facing the north one instead, so from the hall's centre a visitor got 8 px of a 0.9 m picture at 13 m — present, textured, and indistinguishable from art that had failed to load — while every avatar stared down the camera rather than at the person it was pointed at. (The two places that already passed the axis first, backgroundTransform's .dep rotation and NameTag's billboard, were never affected, which is why the tags turned and the furniture did not.) WorldScene.yawTurn(float) is now the only place a heading becomes a matrix, both call sites go through it, and WorldSceneTest asserts the matrix *and* the two vectors that matter — a card's +Z front normal must end up along −X, its width along Z — because the bug raised no exception and a screenshot test needs a display. Re-rendered through the walk-in probe, the two east prints now read as framed landscapes 82 px and 77 px wide from the hall's centre, which is the projection their 0.9 m at 13.3 m predicts.
  • The clinic's hall had no ceiling, because its faces looked the wrong way and nothing asked (wonderland-server) — the shipped room shell is a unit cube whose index lists were hand-edited, and the raster keeps the side a face's geometric normal points at: wound face-up, a ceiling is *culled* from inside the room. Standing in the hall therefore meant looking at the far wall's top edge with sky above it, and the twelve light panels overhead were missing the same way; the floor was its own half-defect, one of its two quads wound face-down so the carpet under a visitor's feet was not drawn at all. The comment in hall-wlc.xml asserted the ceiling "is drawn facing down" while the bytes did the opposite, and ClinicRoomArtTest stayed green throughout because every case it had asks what the shell *contains* — the accessor count, the index range, the five materials, the panel grid — and none asks which way it looks. clinic-room.dae now winds the ceiling and every light panel face-down and both carpet quads face-up (walls and dado already carry a quad on each side, so they read from inside and from the map view), the comment states the rule the bytes now obey, and ClinicRoomArtTest.everySurfaceFacesThePersonStandingInside() walks every triangle of the shell and asserts the sign of its normal per material — including that each material contributed faces, since an empty walk is exactly how this file could pass with no ceiling. Proven both ways: the new case fails against the previously shipped bytes and passes against these, and re-rendered through the walk-in probe the hall closes overhead, the cream panels are seen at the top of the frame, and the carpet is continuous under the avatars.
  • A world's own text read upside down over every head, because one upload inverted and only half the cards were told (wonderland-renderer) — the shared Java 3D texture upload now hands a picture over with its origin at the upper left (yUp = false), which samples the image's first row at v = 1 — the convention the shipped COLLADA exports are authored for, which is why their wall signs and posters read upright. The three cards this file writes by hand still mapped v = 0 to their top edge, so every name tag over every resident, every hung picture card and the sky's own ramp arrived vertically inverted while the art behind them was correct — measured off a rendered clinic, where Waiting Patient and the lobby's Directory came back upside down and the band above the wall got *paler* the higher it rose (177,202,229 overhead against 168,194,225 lower down: a gradient running downhill). WorldScene.tagQuad and WorldScene.flatQuad now carry v = 1 at the top of a card and SkyArt.rowOf puts the ramp's zenith at the box's ceiling, so one stated convention governs every textured primitive the renderer builds; the comments that claimed the opposite — and the WorldSceneTest / SkyArtTest assertions that pinned that claim as CI truth — now state the measured one. Re-rendered: the clinic's names read, the sky deepens overhead (123,159,209 at the top of the frame against 133,167,212 at the horizon), and the combined world's COLLADA grass and paving are unchanged.
  • The Wonderland World panel dead-ended on "Cannot reach", and a seeded world spammed the boot log (lg3d-apps + wonderland-common + wonderland-server) — the desktop deliberately leaves wonderland-server a separate process, so a first launch of the Wonderland World browser always failed with a bare Cannot reach http://localhost:8080/api/world/cells and no way forward. The panel now names the command that brings a server up — ./gradlew :wonderland-server:bootRun --args='--wonderland.world.seed=wonderland-outpatient-clinic' — on the status strip and in its tooltip, from a single WorldCatalog.startCommand() the face and its test share, so the panel is a way in rather than a dead end. Two runtime-noise defects surfaced while verifying it live: CellTransform's non-uniform-scale branch called Thread.dumpStack() alongside its warning, so booting a seeded world printed a full stack trace per cell (the warning, which is the real message, stays); and the outpatient clinic's module.xml and clinic-box.dae used -- as an em dash inside an XML comment, which the spec forbids, so the COLLADA parser logged [Fatal Error] The string "--" is not permitted within comments once per cell — both comments now carry a real em dash. WonderlandWorldPanelTest is updated to assert the strip names both the unreachable server and the start command.
  • The Update Manager's What's New had nothing to show, because its parser did not recognise this repository's changelog (update-manager) — ChangelogManager read ## Version X.Y.Z (YYYY-MM-DD) headers and - [NEW] / - [FIX] / - Breaking change: bullets, the vocabulary of its own unit tests, while CHANGELOG.md — and the changelog.md asset scripts/release/release-notes.sh extracts from it for each Release — is written Keep a Changelog: a ## [X.Y.Z] — date — summary header with ### Added / ### Fixed groups. Its header regex (##\s+(?:Version\s+)?([\d.]+)) cannot match a [, so the document this product ships parses to zero entries: getEntry answered empty, the dialog said "No changelog available", and it said that for every version since the format changed — a feature dead in the water, with a green suite, because the tests fed it the format it was written for rather than the one the repository writes. Both vocabularies are read now: a bracketed header yields its version (a pre-release suffix is kept, and getEntry compares the base version first, then the whole header), the six Keep a Changelog groups map onto the entry's own buckets (Added to features, Fixed and Security to fixes, Changed to changes, Deprecated and Removed to breaking changes), and a bullet outside any group is reported as a change instead of being dropped. [Unreleased] never answers getEntry(version) but does appear in toHtml(), so in-progress work cannot be presented to a user as shipped. Inline markdown now renders instead of showing its own markup: the changelog's **bold**, `code` and links became spans, with code spans following the CommonMark rule — a run of *n* backticks is opened and closed only by a run of exactly *n* — so the ` ```mermaid ` prose in the changelog no longer ate the sentence around it. That rule is implemented twice, here and in scripts/mandela/whats-new.mnd, and pinned by tests on both sides: the same document read in two places must not disagree in either. No public signature changed, so UpdateService, UpdatePresenter and ChangelogDialog needed nothing. The parser is also given a document to parse on a fresh install, which is the half that made the fix invisible without it: releaseBundle now carries CHANGELOG.md renamed changelog.md at the archive root, the generated lg3d.sh passes -Dupdate.changelog.path="${HERE}/changelog.md", and getLocalChangelogPath() resolves configuration, then that system property, then the detected install root, then user.dir — so the notes open offline, before any update server is contacted, while the remote path (version.json → changelog) lands in the same reader. ChangelogManagerTest grows from 16 cases to 28: the real header and group spellings, [Unreleased] refusing a lookup, a faithful excerpt of the shipped changelog yielding entries where the old parser yielded none, the backtick-run edges, and the legacy vocabulary still passing unchanged.
  • No wonderland jar was on the desktop's classpath, so the Wonderland applications shipped since M7a could not run (lg3d-core + lg3d-apps) — lg3d-core's hand-assembled run classpath and its releaseBundle listed every module jar the shell needs by name, and when the wonderland modules were added to the build nobody added them there: grep wonderland lg3d-core/build.gradle returned nothing. Seven lg3d-apps production classes import org.jdesktop.wonderland.* — M7a's JfxMediaSurface, M7b's PdfBoxRasterizer, M7d's ExternalSoftphoneBackend and JavaSoundVoiceBridge, and M6c2's WonderlandWorld3D, WonderlandHudPanel and WorldCatalogInventory — so each died with NoClassDefFoundError: org/jdesktop/wonderland/… the first time a started app touched them: the milestone had reported live sinks that the running desktop could not reach at all. lg3d-apps now declares wonderland-desktop / wonderland-client / wonderland-common (the last two named because wonderland-desktop carries them as non-exposed implementation while its signatures name their types), and both the run task and the release bundle carry the six wonderland jars plus the third-party set they need — JAXB, jakarta.xml.bind-api, reflections and javassist reached through wonderland-common's own runtimeClasspath (so the versions cannot drift from the module's, and lg3d-core is not dragged in twice) — and ice4j through a detached configuration. Verified by diffing the assembled run classpath against :lg3d-apps' own runtimeClasspath: the only entry the desktop lacks is lg3d-core's own jar, which the run task supplies as classes; releaseBundle now contains wonderland-*.jar, ice4j and jaxb-runtime in lib/, which the launcher's lib/* wildcard picks up without a script edit.
  • WorldInputRouter did not read the abstract mouse-motion class as a hover (wonderland-desktop) — the mapping tested MouseMovedEvent3D but lg3d's own hierarchy puts MouseMovedEvent3D and MouseDraggedEvent3D under MouseMotionEvent3D, so a motion event handed over as the class a listener registered — rather than the concrete event's own — fell through to null and the cell silently never heard the gesture. The hover branch now tests the abstract parent (the drag is still answered first, so a drag cannot be misread as a hover, and the wheel still belongs to the scene manager), pinned by WorldInputRouterTest.motionAndEnterBothReadAsHover — the case that found it, and a failure this branch would have shipped.
  • A parsed COLLADA document lost the author's order, and the avatar clip list shuffled itself (wonderland-modules, wonderland-renderer) — ColladaDocument kept every library (animations, effects, visualScenes, geometries, images, materials) as a Map.copyOf copy while its own javadoc promised *parse order*, and ColladaClips.fromDocument documented that its clip map "matches the library's parse order" on top of that. Map.copyOf returns an unordered immutable map: its iteration sequence comes from the keys' hashes and is not specified, so AnimationLibrary.names() (the clip listing), AnimationClip.animatedNodes() / sampleAt() (the sequence the live renderer walks to write the per-node LOCAL transforms) and ColladaDocument.texturePaths() (documented *encounter* order) all silently disagreed with their contract. It bit M7c's AvatarAnimationBundledPoolTest.bodyAclipsParseFromTheShippedBytes, which asks the shipped humanoid-a.dae for [walking, idle] and got [idle, walking] back on some JVM runs and the expected pair on others — a four-in-six failure rate measured on the branch before the fix, i.e. a flaky CI step over what is really an ordering bug. The parsers were already building LinkedHashMaps; the views now wrap them with Collections.unmodifiableMap (same immutability, real document order), so the sequence is fixed by the file rather than by a hash. Pinned by the new AnimationLibraryTest.clipAndNodeOrderIsTheAuthorsNotTheHashesOfTheNames, which asserts the guarantee at all three levels — catalog, clip, and two <animation> elements parsed end to end — with names chosen so a hash order would differ from the written order.
  • indexOf now honours its start index instead of ignoring it (lg3d-mandela, rt/StandardLibrary) — s.indexOf(needle, from) read only args[0], so it answered the *first* occurrence and called it the answer: a script asking for the closing quote after the opening one got the opening one back, no error, and a wrong number. Found while writing Mandela at Work, whose demo printed "0 wired gate task(s)" until the scan was bisected (measured before the fix: both calls returned index 13 on the same line). Both spellings are fixed together — Str.indexOf and List.indexOf — because leaving the start index honoured in one and ignored in the other would have kept the defect and only moved it. The rules are the ones a Java-shaped surface promises: a negative start is 0 and not a count from the end, so the -1 a failed lookup answers cannot scramble the search that follows it; a start past the end answers -1 rather than refusing; a Long too big for an index is clamped instead of wrapping ("a-b-c".indexOf("c", 9223372036854775807) is -1, not a crash and not a wrong hit); a non-number is the TypeError the rest of the library raises. Thirteen new cases in StandardLibraryTest pin every branch through the public facade, including the scanner idiom the page now teaches (t.indexOf("'", t.indexOf("'") + 1) is the *second* quote), and §9 of the language guide documents the argument where the member table previously listed only the name. No shipped script passed a second argument, so nothing in the tree was relying on the old behaviour; the page's demo was rewritten to the direct call and its transcript re-run, which is byte-identical apart from the timestamp — the fix changes the call, not the answer the workaround had been forced to reach.
  • The release train no longer cuts releases by itself (.github/workflows/release-train.yml) — a merge to main could complete the one open milestone and the train then auto-cut a release/X.Y.Z branch without any human deciding to ship; with the RELEASE_PAT secret absent the cut died halfway (the release PR cannot be created by GITHUB_TOKEN), leaving orphan stale branches — three of them, release/1.67.0, release/1.68.1 and release/1.69.0, accumulated before this fix. The root confusion was a stale milestone title (1.28.0, open since September, permanently "complete") that sync-milestone reused without checking it against the derived version. Now cut-rc fires only on an explicit workflow_dispatch, the merge-assign job no longer dispatches a release re-evaluation, the daily schedule is bookkeeping only, and sync-milestone renames a drifted milestone title to the derived version. The canonical release path is the local ./make-release.sh, which pushes the annotated tag with real credentials so release.yml actually publishes — documented as such in docs/release-process.md.
  • A class's construction counts its initialiser's parameters, not its fields (lg3d-mandela, vm/VM) — class Box { var v = 1 } has one field and takes no argument, but the upper bound of the count was read off the declaration's field list, so Box(42) was accepted and overwrote the body's default. The refusal now names the count the author wrote, and a named call that leaves a required field with no default as a hole is refused on that field's name instead of handing the machine's own <absent> marker to the body. Pinned by MachineDispatchTest.
  • The host re-entrancy limit reports the depth that was reached (lg3d-mandela, vm/VM) — the sentence was built after the counter was restored to the outer frame, so it understated the recursion by one and pointed a host tuning its budget at a number that would have been enough; the allowed budget is now named in the message too. Pinned by MachineHostTest.
  • An Int operation that overflows promotes to Double instead of answering with its left operand (lg3d-mandela, values/Operators) — the promotion branch had been written as an expression that cancelled the right-hand side away, so 1 + 9223372036854775807 answered 1.0; 2 ** 63 let a raw ArithmeticException escape the language's error model and print a Java stack trace. The documented rule is now in the guide and pinned by ArithmeticOverflowTest.
  • A closure can capture a variable owned by a grandparent function (lg3d-mandela, code/Compiler) — the intermediate leg of the capture chain was never emitted, so a closure built two functions below the one that owns the name read a slot its own frame does not have and the machine died with ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. Pinned by ClosureCaptureTest.
  • The guide described a range as exclusive of its end (docs/mandela-language.md) — the machine has always answered 5 for (1..5).length, as MandelaRange and OperatorRulesTest agree, while the prose said a..b stops before b. A reader following the sentence would have written 1..n for a loop that must not overshoot; the guide now states the inclusive rule and names a..<b> as the exclusive form.
  • A host function's Java answer is converted at the machine, like a bound name is (lg3d-mandela, vm/VM) — HostFunction.of("count", 1, args -> text.length()) is the shape the embedding guide tells a host to write, and length() answers a Java int. The call pushed it unchanged, so the script held a value the language has no name for: typeOf(...) answered Host, count("abc") == 3 was false (Integer.equals(Long)), 1 + count("abc") was a TypeError, and a member read off the number fell through to a raw java.lang.Integer path that no script could tell was there. The documented conversion table is now applied by VM.callHost itself, which also means an object with no Mandela form is refused with its class named instead of handed to the script. Pinned by HostBoundaryTest; the two instanceof Integer accommodations in StandardLibrary are gone with it, one of which (whole(...)) answered 0 for any Integer it was given.
  • A bare ## [Unreleased] header no longer turns release-check red (scripts/mandela/release-check.mnd) — the gate read the version out of the CHANGELOG's *first* ## [ header, so the legitimate state between a release cut and the next bump chore — a feature branch opening an unnamed [Unreleased] section above the newest release — was reported as a self-contradictory repository (CHANGELOG.md says Unreleased, build.gradle says 1.68.0). It now walks the headers and returns the first one that actually carries a version, so :lg3d-mandela:repositoryChecks is green in all three states a branch moves through: released, development (## [Unreleased] — 1.69.0-dev) and in-between.
  • std.json refuses the numbers RFC 8259 refuses (lg3d-mandela, rt/Json) — the reader's own javadoc says it "stays strict on purpose, because a document that two parsers disagree about is a bug nobody can find later", but it read 01 as the Int 1. A hand-written settings file, or an octal-looking literal from a lenient producer, therefore parsed here and failed (or parsed as a different value) at the other end of the wire; json.isValid answered true for it, which is the worse half, since a script that validates before parsing was told the document was JSON. A second digit after a 0 is now a JsonError naming the line and column.
  • A Java value handed to the writer crosses the table the machine uses (lg3d-mandela, rt/Json) — Json.encode and Json.stringify are public Java entry points, and the writer special-cased exactly one host type, Integer. So Json.encode("abc".length()) answered 3 while Json.encode(1.5f), Json.encode(List.of(1, 2)) and Json.stringify(Map.of("k", "v")) all raised *json cannot encode a Host* — an arbitrary line for a host, and the same leak VM.callHost was just fixed for. The writer now runs its input through the documented widening at every node, which is what lets the Integer special case go away.
  • A wide Double is written with a signed exponent (lg3d-mandela, rt/Json) — the language's own number rendering keeps an exponent for a value too wide for plain digits, and Java spells that form as 1.0E16 while the JSON grammar requires a sign on the exponent. json.encode(1e16) therefore produced a document this reader accepts and a stricter one rejects; it now writes 1.0E+16. All three are pinned by the new JsonTest (113 cases), which takes rt/Json from no suite at all to every line and branch of it covered.
  • abs of the most negative Int promotes instead of wrapping (lg3d-mandela, rt/StandardLibrary) — Math.abs(Long.MIN_VALUE) is Long.MIN_VALUE, so abs(0 - 9223372036854775807 - 1) answered the same negative number it was handed, the exact roll-over the guide promises an Int never suffers. It now answers Double, the way the unary minus already did at that edge.
  • padStart/padEnd honour the text ceiling repeat already enforced (lg3d-mandela, rt/StandardLibrary) — the ceiling was applied to the builder's *capacity*, not to the loop, so "x".padStart(20000000, "0") built the 20-million-character string instead of refusing it; a width read off a bad value was a heap eat, not a LimitError.
  • int(...) refuses a double with no Int instead of saturating (lg3d-mandela, rt/StandardLibrary) — longValue() answers MAX_VALUE for any double past the range, so int(math.pow(2, 63)) quietly returned a number that was not the one asked for. Outside -2**63 … 2**63-1 is now a LimitError, the same shape the size ceilings answer.
  • A Range offers only the copying sorting spellings (lg3d-mandela, rt/StandardLibrary) — the delegating table registered the mutating sortBy name but the copying sortedBy body, so range.sortedBy(…) was an unknown member while range.sortBy(…) "worked" by reordering a throwaway materialised copy and answering it — a sort that could never change the range. The delegation now spells sortedBy, sortBy is not a Range member (a TypeError like any unknown member), and the guide's table matches.
  • A call missing its second argument is told it needs two (lg3d-mandela, rt/StandardLibrary) — the two argument helpers spelled the same sentence separately, and the numbered branch read "needs its 2th argument". The shared spelling says how many arguments the call needs.
  • A downward Range lost its last value (lg3d-mandela, values/MandelaRange) — the count added the inclusive end's unit in the *bounds'* direction instead of the *stride's*, so every range that counts down was one value short: 8..0 step -1 walked 8 to 2, answered 7 for .length and 2 for .last, and printed eight numbers in a for loop while 0 in (8..0 step -1) said true underneath it. (5..1 step -1).sum() answered 12 where the closed form the library uses says 15. The count is now measured along the stride, so .length, .last, toList(), for and in are one answer in both directions — and the bounds are still never overflowed: a span a long cannot name answers MAX_VALUE as "more than a count" rather than a negative number. Pinned by IterationTest; the two LanguageTest expectations that had encoded the old rule, with a comment rationalising it as ceil(7 / 2), are corrected with it.
  • == compared only the top level of a container (lg3d-mandela, values/MandelaList, MandelaMap, MandelaInstance) — each element was asked through Java's Object.equals, so [1] == [1.0] was false while 1 == 1.0 is true, json.parse("[1.0]") == [1] was false for a document read off the wire, 1.0 in [1] and [1] in [[1.0]] were false, distinct() kept what the language calls one value twice, and P(1) == P(1.0) disagreed with the record's own structural promise. There is now one equality, Values.equal, and every container delegates to it per element.
  • A container's hash disagreed with its equality (lg3d-mandela, values), the other half of the same bug: 1 and 1.0 are equal but hashed apart, so a script that used a List as a set or a map key got a different bucket for the same value. Values.hash is the canonical hash for every value — a number hashes as a double whichever side it arrived on, a map ignores its insertion order, a type instance hashes its fields — and the three containers delegate to it.
  • Two Doubles that are the same number were unequal (lg3d-mandela, values/Values) — -0.0 == 0.0 answered false while -0.0 < 0.0 answered true, an equality and an ordering that cannot both be right, and a NaN was never told about at all. Numbers compare by value, so -0.0 and 0.0 are one number, with the one documented exception that NaN equals itself: that is what lets distinct() answer [1, 2, NaN] for [1, 2, NaN, NaN] instead of keeping a value the script cannot tell apart.
  • A big Int comparison collapsed two distinct numbers (lg3d-mandela, values/Values) — ordering converted both sides to double, so 9223372036854775807 > 9223372036854775806 answered false and sorted() could reorder a list == calls equal. Two Ints are compared with Long.compare, and only a real Double in the pair takes the floating path.
  • A Double was printed with placeholder zeros (lg3d-mandela, values/Values) — 1e-6 displayed as 0.0000010, breaking the promise formatDouble's own javadoc makes (the shortest decimal that round-trips) and putting text on the console that a reader cannot paste back as the value it came from. The placeholder digits are stripped; a whole Double still keeps its .0.
  • x as Any returned the text of the value (lg3d-mandela, values/Values) — the Any branch of the conversion table shared the Str path, so 42 as Any handed back "42": a conversion that silently changed the type the rest of the program tests with is. Any asks for no shape, so it is now the identity.

Changed

  • The lg3d-webserver floors are raised to 0.985 line / 0.975 branch and 82 mutants (build.gradle, lg3d-webserver) — the Spring Boot management server's coverage ratchet sat at the conservative 0.890 / 0.795 it was given when the module landed, and its mutation floor at 78. A fault-injection campaign drives the pure core to every line and branch reachable in-JVM — measured 99.02-99.16% / 98.10% and 83% mutation (317 of 380 mutants detected) — so both floors follow the measurement. The new cases reach DeploymentRegistry's defensive catch arms through a fault-injecting StubBackend (a deploy/start/stop/remove/isRunning that throws DeploymentException vs RuntimeException) and an orphan registry whose persisted app has no backend; DockerDeploymentBackend's detail-message fallbacks over blank, negative-exit and null streams; ReverseProxyFilter's 502-on-interrupt, committed-response skip and null/hop-by-hop header drop against an in-JVM com.sun.net.httpserver; and the real RealProcessLauncher / RealChildProcessStarter interrupt, bounded-window and SIGTERM-escalation paths over genuine short-lived children. Two dead-code removals fell out of reaching every branch: requirePortFree / requireContextPathFree carried a selfId parameter every caller passed null (a pre-insert check has no self to exclude), and newId / deriveName / deriveContextPath each guarded a blank slug that validate() and slug()'s own "app-" fallback already make unreachable — both now a comment naming the invariant instead of a branch no test could kill. The residue is branches genuinely unreachable in-JVM (WebServerApplication.main, JarProcessBackend.javaExecutable's Windows fallback, RealProcessLauncher's joinQuietly interrupt, ReverseProxyFilter's contractually-never-null guards); of the 63 unkilled mutants only 3 are NO_COVERAGE and the other 60 SURVIVED sit on covered lines whose tests assert the outcome but not the exact mutated token inside a detail message.
  • The world browser previews through JOGL by default (lg3d-apps) — WorldRender.joglPreviewEnabled() inverts from opt-in to opt-out: the JOGL preview path (GlWorldBuilder into a GlWorldViewer) is now the shipped desktop's default renderer for the world browser's vignette instead of the java3d WorldViewer, which PR #412 proved at parity across all eight worlds once DepthBlitFormat matched the framebuffer's 32-bit-float depth. Set -Dlg.wonderland.jogl=false as the escape hatch back to the java3d viewer while it still exists; both paths keep the identical Attempt contract (a missing frame is a reason, never an exception) and both check hasGeometry first, so only tryPreview's dispatch changes. The java3d WorldViewer is not removed here — WorldRender.open()'s interactive walk-in view and the 3D desktop's WonderlandWorldContainer still need it, so the cutover continues with a JOGL interactive viewer before those files and the java3d-core dependency go. WorldRenderTest.joglPreviewIsTheDefault pins the new default-on / explicit-false semantics.
  • The clinic is one building, not eight boxes on a field (wonderland-server) — see the Fixed entry above for the authoring bug this re-tile exposed; the layout is the answer to a plainer complaint. The hall got furnished and the rooms were still *placed* rather than *built*: six 4 m shells at arbitrary offsets outside the lobby's own walls, with a floor the size of a parking lot under them — which is what a visitor reads as a diorama of models rather than as the clinic in outpatientclinic.jpg.
